articles.title: Op-Ed: Building Toward a Greener, Housing-Abundant Seattle
articles.author: Logan Schmidt
paras: There’s a reason Seattle is called the Emerald City in the Evergreen State: our trees help make Seattle the vibrant city that it is. But preserving that vision doesn’t mean we have to choose between protecting them and building the housing we need. We can – and must – do both.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

In 2007, Seattle established a goal to reach 30% tree canopy coverage by 2037. At the time, the city’s canopy stood at 18%, according to the City’s Urban Forestry Management Plan . To reach their goal, the City of Seattle Urban Forestry Coalition – consisting of an interdepartmental team of staff from Seattle Parks and Recreation, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), the Office of Sustainability and the Environment, and more – put forth a list of short and long-term actions, including improving planting and maintenance of City-managed trees, strengthening incentives and regulations to encourage tree preservation on private property, and exploring new financing mechanisms to fund City-operated urban forestry programs.

Seattle has made strong progress toward that goal: the most recent tree canopy study , using data from 2021, has Seattle at 28.1% canopy coverage, an increase of 10 percentage points in 14 years – even as the city’s population grew by nearly 150,000 people and added more than 100,000 new units of housing. As the city prepares for more growth, we have an opportunity to develop new policies and investments to close the remaining gap and meet or even exceed the City’s 30% goal.

And while we continue to care for trees and our environment, Seattle is also grappling with a serious housing shortage. Under the One Seattle Plan ’s adopted growth targets, Seattle must plan for 120,000 new housing units by 2044, or roughly 6,000 homes per year.

Since 2017, Seattle added 8,300 new homes in the Neighborhood Residential (formerly Single Family) zone, typically where detached, ADUs, and moderate middle housing products are built. In lowrise, midrise, highrise, and downtown zones, where apartments are more prevalent, 27,500 units were added. However, data shows a significant downturn in permits in 2025 and 2026, which is a concerning reality for what’s to come, considering new housing takes years to move from permit to construction to occupancy.

The slowing production of housing will only further place strain on homeowners and renters in the city. Seattle homebuyers spent 54.1% of their income on housing costs in 2024, making it one of the least affordable housing markets in the country. And nearly 50% of renter households in the region are cost burdened , meaning they're paying more than 30% of their income on rent.

So, how are we, as a city and region, responding to this pressure? Well, the answer is two-fold. The One Seattle Plan is both Seattle’s Comprehensive Plan – the 20-year vision and roadmap for the city’s growth, required under Washington’s Growth Management Act (GMA) – and the vehicle through which Seattle adopted middle housing: duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes, and other “ missing middle ” housing types mandated statewide by House Bill 1110 . In other words, the same document that guides how Seattle grows responsibly is also the one legalizing more homes in more neighborhoods.

However, the GMA doesn’t just require cities like Seattle to develop comprehensive plans and regulations to guide their growth. It requires local governments to treat housing, transportation, the environment, and more as coequal goals, not competing ones.

Despite this requirement, in public debates at City Hall, goals like more housing and the environment are seemingly – and incorrectly so – pitted against each other. Seattle’s own Urban Forestry Commission has pushed back on the notion that urban density and tree canopy cannot coexist, noting that “what we need to do is better understand how we balance one and the other, while acknowledging that both are necessary.”

Why does the conversation then so often fall into a choice between the two? And instead of asking whether we can have housing or trees, maybe it’s worth asking: what policy choices let us have both ? That starts with recognizing Seattle’s role in the broader region and building on the approaches already showing that density and canopy can grow together.

When cities enact policies that limit opportunities for new housing, that new development doesn't stop – it just moves elsewhere. And that prevents people who want to live and work in a city like Seattle from accessing homes in the transit-oriented, walkable neighborhoods Seattleites and our local government have spent years investing in. Pushing people further out into car-dependent areas results in longer commutes, more vehicle miles traveled, and more emissions. It also means more roads and parking lots replacing permeable land, sending stormwater runoff into local waterways, and further harming our salmon and orca populations .

Furthermore, building new housing in the city can make our current urban environment better. According to a recent King County study of Lake Washington , from 2000 to 2020, the population of the watershed grew by 34% while developed land area grew by less than 5% and forest cover remained steady. Rather than clearing intact forest to accommodate growth, the population grew in place by converting from lower-density to higher-density housing. This new development likely prompted stormwater upgrades, septic-to-sewer transitions, and other changes that helped improve the lake’s water quality.

Not only have we seen improvements in the lake’s water quality, but we’ve also seen new construction lead to planting and protecting trees on site at a rate 325% higher than tree removals are occurring. Since July 2023, when Seattle’s Tree Protection Ordinance went into effect, more than 14,100 trees have been planted and protected during the construction of new homes compared to roughly 4,300 trees removed.

Of those trees removed during construction, nearly 88% were a Tier 3, Tier 4, or below category. The majority of the older, larger tree loss is happening entirely outside of construction: nearly 71% of all Tier 2 tree removals are non-construction-related (Tier 2 trees include trees 24 inches or greater, tree groves, and specific tree species as provided by a Director’s Rule ).

We continue to be interested in finding more ways to preserve and add trees alongside the construction of new housing. However, if protecting Seattle’s most significant trees is the goal, the data points toward paying more attention to the far larger share of removals occurring with no new housing to show for it.

Even worse, and not accounted for in the data above, the largest net change in Seattle’s canopy coverage between 2016 and 2021 occurred in publicly owned parks (“Parks Natural Areas”). Seattle’s parks saw a 5.1% canopy loss, accounting for nearly half of the city’s overall canopy loss (111 of the 255 acres lost) across all management types (neighborhood residential, right-of-way, etc.).

The public right-of-way didn’t fare much better. Over that same period, the city lost 10 acres of canopy in the right-of-way alone – land the city already owns and controls, and the same land that makes up 27% of Seattle’s total area . This points exactly to where the opportunity is: parks and the public right-of-way represent the few places the city can take action on to impact canopy growth directly.

Everyone who cares about housing and trees needs to continue to work on creative solutions for both. Many of our members continue to do that and we look forward to hearing new ideas. In the meantime, we already have solutions we can start implementing now. If new housing isn’t the leading culprit for Seattle’s canopy loss, then we should be putting less energy into pitting homebuilding against trees amidst a regional housing shortage. Rather, it’s time to get serious about growing canopy everywhere. Seattle’s already set the target: 30% canopy by 2037. Getting there means treating tree planting like the public priority it actually is.
Here’s are strategies we can start implementing now:

None of this requires choosing between a growing city and a green one – the data backs that up, and the Complete Communities Coalition laid out the case in more detail in their fact sheet, Right Tree, Right Place: A Greener, Housing-Abundant Seattle .

articles.title: ‘Less of the dissertation’ — Hollingsworth backs big business demands for 100-day Seattle public safety plan
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: You can watch the Hollingsworth interview here
Seattle City Council President Joy Hollingsworth is backing demands from a coalition of major Seattle-area employers calling for the city to produce a comprehensive 100-day public safety action plan.

In her appearance Friday on a talk radio news show on KIRO FM , Hollingsworth took jabs at Mayor Katie Wilson and city leaders she says depend too much on theoretical discussions over visible enforcement.

“There have been too many people in this city that have workshopped their public safety dissertations on communities, right now,” Hollingsworth said during the KIRO appearance. “Well, let’s pull this lever. Well, what if we turn this off? What if we do this? You’re listening to the people right now, and they’re telling you to their face: ‘This is what we want. We want a positive relationship with our police officers. We want gun violence prevention programs to work for us. We want after-school programs.’ They’re telling us everything they want.”

Hollingsworth thanked the business leaders for keeping their companies anchored locally rather than abandoning the city. “They could have did us like the Baltimore Colts did. When the football team woke up in the middle of the night and just left,” she said.

CHS reported Friday on the letter organized by the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and signed by leadership at companies including Microsoft, Starbucks, Costco, and Alaska Airlines calling on Wilson to create an immediate “100-day public safety action plan” with “concrete” performance metrics, just ahead of fall city budget debates. The letter cites low officer totals, slow 911 response times, and the stalled expansion of SPD’s Real Time Crime Center camera system as issues that require immediate response and cites an August Chamber survey where only 34% of 500 registered voters expressed confidence in Seattle’s public safety approach.
CHS reached out to Hollingsworth’s office for her response to the letter but the District 3 leader elected in 2023 with support from then-Mayor Bruce Harrell took to the airwaves Friday instead,

Addressing the public safety strategy survey, Hollingsworth said the metric indicates “people don’t trust us, potentially, to execute certain things.” She endorsed employer priorities—including active CCTV surveillance and increased police presence—while emphasizing that she tracks outcomes through five indicators: police response times, encampment activity, overdose deaths, crime categories, and victim vulnerability.

Wilson responded to the letter by defending ongoing municipal initiatives, saying the city doubled crisis responder hours and bolstered police presence across key neighborhoods. “Seattle is making progress, step by step,” Wilson said, pointing to decade-low shooting and homicide rates while acknowledging that “we have far too much crime and public disorder, and people have a right to be frustrated.”
he business coalition’s public safety push arrives as Wilson faces a looming budget deficit and explores expanding progressive taxes on large employers.

Wilson has prioritized civilian alternatives, harm reduction, and administrative accountability over traditional police expansion — forcing out Chief Shon Barnes , targeting hotspot patrols, and freezing surveillance camera expansion.
The council president and the Pike/Pine clean-up crew (Image: @cmjoyhollings )

Hollingsworth has been critical of the Barnes decision and has typically taken a middle ground approach on public safety, balancing police staffing and deterrence tools like Stay Out of Drug Areas zones with the civilian CARE department, community violence intervention at Garfield High School , and localized business improvement resources.

Last week, Hollingsworth lauded the work of one of the budget investments she says she advocated for in last year’s budget process to help address public safety issues in the Pike/Pine neighborhood — a new “Pike/Pine street cleaning crew out there at 7am picking up litter, power washing sidewalks.”
Hollingsworth said Friday that the City Council remains “willing and ready to work with the mayor” to achieve safety results, concluding: “I need to see action. I need to see boots on the ground.”
“I need to see people with active actions and less of the planning and the dissertation and the workshop of that.”

articles.title: ‘But enough about you …’ How to survive in a world of monologuists, interrupters and trauma dumpers
articles.author: Anita Chaudhuri
paras: Conversations are supposed to be two-sided – but all too often we come up against someone who’s passionately, exclusively in love with the sound of their own voice. Time to fight back …

When I was in my early teens, I was often invited round to a schoolfriend’s house for dinner. Her family struck me as wildly progressive: they were Danish and indulged in all sorts of “out-there” activities – fondues, candle-making and, most terrifying of all, the talking stick. Before the meal was served, someone would retrieve the sacred broom handle and it would be passed around the table. You could speak only if you had possession of the stick. Despite it being the most stressful thing ever (it meant being in the spotlight, and then remembering to keep quiet the rest of the time), I now frequently yearn for a more convenient version of that stick. For example, I met a friend recently who I see infrequently but keep up with via voice notes. No sooner had we sat down than he launched into a long discourse about his new marathon training food plan. He only broke the flow to order an omelette: “Four egg whites, two yolks, is that possible?” (We were in my local greasy spoon, so the request was greeted with mirth.) When we left, 90 minutes later, he finally had the grace to turn to me and ask: “And how are things with you?” Walking home, I felt a mixture of disappointment and irritation. Had he always been so self-absorbed? So uninterested in anyone else? I couldn’t help wondering if our one-sided virtual updates had played a part in the problem. There is a name for this type of egocentric behaviour – “conversational narcissism”. Although it was coined by the sociologist Charles Derber in his 1979 book The Pursuit of Attention, the term seems more relevant than ever. “WhatsApp communication and voice notes are really a series of monologues,” says Charlotte Fox Weber, a psychotherapist. “In face-to-face situations, people are forgetting how to pause naturally, to make space to hear and listen. And people are chatting on the phone – an activity that at least requires turn-taking in a defined way – much less often.” A lot of our communication online can feel weirdly transactional, focused on logistics or niche WhatsApp groups. According to Tamu Thomas, a life coach and author, this has damaged the art of improvised conversation. “People have less capacity for meandering conversations that don’t have a purpose,” she says. “A good dialogue is a back-and-forth between two people discovering new things about each other, even if they have known each other for years. Because there are now so many different channels available to stay in touch, some people are confusing communication with connection.” Knowledge is power, though. If you can recognise the five types of common conversation hogger, it will be much easier to handle them.

articles.title: “Hop On Board!” Campaign Kicks Off
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Yesterday, a coalition of transit advocates launched “Hop On Board!”, the official campaign urging Seattle voters to pass the renewal and expansion of the Seattle Transit Measure this November . Speakers at the event included Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, ATU 587 President Greg Woodfill, Nondrivers Alliance founder Anna Zivarts, Transit Riders Union General Manager Lam Ho, and Transportation Choices Coalition ‘s Executive Director Kirk Hovenkotter and Policy Director Katy Ricchiuto.

The Transportation Choices Coalition is leading local advocates pushing for expansion of the transit measure, which proposes to increase the current 0.15% sales tax for transit to 0.3%, the maximum allowed under recently adopted state law. If approved by voters, the measure would take effect in April 2027.

King County Metro uses an equity framework to distribute service across King County but cities have the ability to purchase additional service. Seattle has been buying additional service since 2014 , which brought frequent buses to most of the city and dramatically increased the viability of living car-free.

The current Seattle Transit Measure funds over 7% of all bus trips currently running in Seattle, mainly boosting service along key corridors during the day and providing the majority of Metro’s Night Owl service in the city. The expanded STM would further boost service at night and on weekends, as well as more than doubling the number of free ORCA cards for those who need it and providing funding for several important accessibility programs. The measure also includes funding for capital funding for bus lanes.

At the event, speakers shared stories of how important transit is to their lives and how this measure would make public transit in Seattle more useful for more people. Mayor Wilson focused on the importance of late night bus service to help service workers get home at the end of a late shift without using a rideshare service like Uber or Lyft, or making it possible for a family with two cars to only need one.

Councilmember Rinck shared stories of three-seat rides to Tumwater and the importance of frequent, reliable service, and also highlighted the expanded late night service provided by the measure. Greg Woodfill posited that although sales taxes are regressive, this measure’s taxes will go right back to serving the people who need it most, stating “every $1 spent on transit is $5 back in the community”. Anna Zivarts stressed the importantance of frequent and reliable service to those who cannot drive, and how the transit measure would bring more service to more communities. Zivarts put it simply: “transit is freedom”. Other speakers highlighted the proposed increase in free ORCA passes for low-income riders and the elderly, and the importance of pushing back against likely opposition to the measure.
If you are intersested in supporting the Hop On Board campaign, you can sign up to volunteer for upcoming events , or donate to the campaign .

articles.title: Environmental Complaints Against Seattle Growth Plan Thrown Out in State Ruling
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The City of Seattle has some updates to make to the environmental review used to update its 20-year housing and jobs growth plan, but claims alleging that corners were cut when conducting that review were mostly thrown out this week in a ruling from Washington's Growth Management Hearings Board (GMHB).
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Wednesday's ruling came in response to a set of two appeals filed against the final environmental impact statement (FEIS) for former mayor Bruce Harrell's One Seattle Comprehensive Plan update. The 1,300-page document reviewed impacts from expanding the city's zoning capacity to allow denser development, particularly along transit corridors and in tight clusters close to existing business districts.

These GMHB appeals are separate from the pair of City-level FEIS appeals that have been advancing through the state court system; those are still pending after the Washington Court of Appeals ruled that they should be able to move forward. It's those challenges that are currently holding up implementation of the Comprehensive Plan's second phase, now pushed to at least early 2027.

There is some overlap, however. One of the appeals ruled on this week was filed by Jennifer Godfrey, the Seattle Symphony musician who challenged the FEIS at the city level last year and took her appeal all the way to the Washington Court of Appeals. Godfrey alleged that the plan did not adequately address concerns around the impact of polluted stormwater runoff on Puget Sound's population of Southern Resident killer whales (SRKW). The "Orca Appeal" has attracted significant media attention while Godfrey also pursued this parallel avenue to challenge the FEIS, joined by groups including the Orca Conservatory, the Orca Network, and the Puget Sound Harvesters Association. Collectively that group was referred to as the Joint Petitioners by the hearings board.

Godfrey's appeal argued that the One Seattle Plan sets lofty policies regarding tree canopy preservation and water-quality protection, but that the regulations that are tasked with implementing those policies aren't shown to be in alignment with those policies. But the board ruled that no evidence had been presented to show that this was the case.

"The Board disagrees that it was the City’s burden to show how its implementing regulations ' comply' with its policies," the ruling stated. "Instead, it was Joint Petitioners’ burden to show how the implementing regulations are inconsistent with the policies. But Joint Petitioners did not discuss even a single line of text from the implementing regulations, anywhere in their brief, and so fail to meet their burden."

In issuing its final ruling the board found that Seattle had adequately reviewed the potential impacts of housing growth over the next 20 years, it just didn't encompass enough potential growth. It ultimately ruled the FEIS was inadequate because the City had only reviewed the impacts of what is considered "maximum likely development" instead of "maximum possible development" – a move that leaves out approximately 42,000 potential units of housing based on City planners' estimates.

The City argued that considering the impact of development that is unlikely would be speculative, and thus not required under the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) but the growth board did not agree with that either.

"The Board is cognizant of the rule that speculative environmental impacts do not need to be analyzed. It is tempting to think that if additional housing units beyond 120,000 new units are unlikely to be built, then their environmental impacts must be speculative," the ruling said. "That was the logic underlying the City’s decision to limit its environmental analysis to the 120,000 new units it thought were likely under the Update Ordinances, rather than the new development capacity of 162,847 potential new units which the Update Ordinances added to the baseline capacity, or the final capacity of 330,933 potential new units. However, the Board believes that SEPA caselaw distinguishes between impacts that are speculative versus development that is speculative."

During the earlier public comment period, urbanists and housing advocates had raised the point that the City's growth targets appeared on the low side . Divided over 20 years, 120,000 is just 6,000 units added per year, which Seattle has managed to exceed on a regular basis over the recent decade.
But on the underlying environmental analysis for the growth that was studied, the hearings board essentially gave the City its stamp of approval.

"The Board finds that Joint Petitioners have not shown the City failed to use the best available science. The FEIS was deficient for its scope, but not for the quality of the scientific information it relied upon," the ruling stated.

The second GMHB appeal, filed by civil engineer (and past Urbanist contributor ) Donna Breske, dealt with the City of Seattle's plans for water infrastructure, and was fully dismissed. Unlike in Godfrey's appeal, Breske's appeal didn't seek to invalidate any ordinance, but rather force the city to overhaul the Comprehensive Plan's Capital Facilities element to address the current unpredictability of the water permitting process.

The City of Seattle now has a full year to update the One Seattle plan's FEIS to address the potential impacts of the additional units, when it was already in the process of conducting environmental review of even more added density as part of mayor Katie Wilson's pivot from the One Seattle Plan – which has been branded " Taller Denser Faster ."

"[A]s the Board has been at pains to repeat, the FEIS’s environmental analysis would have been adequate [emphasis theirs] if the maximum potential development as a result of the Update Ordinances had been 120,000 new units," the ruling said. "For any amount of growth below this threshold, the FEIS is already adequate . It is only if growth were to exceed the 120,000 new unit threshold that the impacts would not have been considered and mitigated in the FEIS."

The larger issue surrounding Seattle's Comprehensive Plan is what happens with Godfrey's other appeal, which has been moving forward with an appeal filed by Mount Baker resident John M. Cary. Earlier this summer, the Seattle City Council passed a new law that closes off the avenue of appeals to the city hearings examiner when it comes to areawide rezones or updates to the Comprehensive Plan just like this one. That means that it will likely be left to King County Superior Court to adjudicate, with the Council free to consider and adopt the modest rezones that had been on deck before things were put on hold .
While there's no telling how that appeal will ultimately play out, this week's hearings board ruling could provide a preview.

articles.title: Na Hong-jin’s Hope Isn’t Being Advertised as the Blockbuster Troll It Really Is
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: I have seen reviews of Hope bewildered by its third act, confused as to how the competent action movie they were enjoying could culminate in such an awful conclusion. Why did director Na Hong-jin botch the landing? Is he stupid? No. The bad ending is the point. It’s satire and Na is trolling the audience for fun.

Hope is being sold as typical sci-fi action fare from a Korean master of suspense because the studios don’t want to admit that he played an expensive joke on them and they’re desperate to make their production costs back. Or they’re in on the joke and happy to go along with the deception that is the first couple acts of Na’s film. Maybe a bit of both. Whatever gets butts in seats.

At ₩100 billion won—roughly $74 million—this is the most expensive Korean movie ever produced, and it seems Na has intentionally mocked spending so much money on a sci-fi blockbuster franchise by burning the cash while hinting at a sequel he has no interest in making.
It’s as if he’s saying, “Oh you want to hire me, an actual artist, to make an expensive mainstream sci-fi action slop franchise for you? For stupid American hogs? Sure, I’d love to. “

Na is a talented director, and plays the story of a small town attacked by a monster perfectly straight at first. The townsfolk unite to hunt it down, but there’s something even more mysterious in the woods, a spooky mystery is afoot! You may or may not see him beginning to dissect genre tropes depending on what you’re expecting going into the theater, but what he’s doing becomes clearer the closer you get to the end.

Na’s scripts have always been deeply cynical, particularly in their resolutions—the pimp tracks down the serial killer, but not before his sex worker is murdered ( The Chaser ) the debtor pays off his liability by completing the assassination, but bleeds to death before finding his missing wife ( The Yellow Sea ), the policeman identifies the demon possessing his daughter, but is tricked by it into suspecting another and killed by her ( The Wailing ). Hope is so cynical that the conclusion itself becomes the punchline to a dry, two-and-a-half hour joke. Everyone in the theater either started laughing or got really pissed off. Some of those laughing seemed in on the joke, other laughers thought Na did a comically bad job, and the angry people agreed with them.

The film starts ordinarily enough with Na’s typical bumbling police characters, tense editing, ultraviolence, and plot signposts pointing to a satisfying conclusion Hope never delivers. By the end, you realize this movie about a fishing village is full of red herrings, and the troll onscreen isn’t the biggest one in the theater with you.

The studios calling in a critically successful genre director to make a lucrative mainstream sci-fi epic is a trend that’s only gotten worse in recent years. Those movies often turn out pretty bad (Richard Kelly’s Southland Tales , Chloe Zhao’s The Eternals ), and Na is at least willing to shoot his own dog. Rian Johnson getting dragged in to try to salvage Disney’s botched Star Wars reboot comes to mind, and at the very least, Na will hopefully make Hope’s budget back and be similarly rewarded with the creative freedom to make his little detective movies. He’s too good for blockbuster schlock and Hope is him showing us.

Many directors have spited studio heads and audiences to make a point. This isn’t William Friedkin or Michael Cimino breaking the bank with Sorcerer and Days of Heaven and fighting the studio on an ultimately good movie sold poorly to audiences. This is Tom Green getting hired to make a mainstream comedy by executives who don’t understand his humor and delivering, to their horror, the anti-art Freddy Got Fingered . Hope’s self-destructive third act meta-narrative owes more to Alex Cox’s in Walker than a failure to deliver on Na’s part.

If you want a more stereotypical Korean action horror film you should see Colony instead, it’s in theaters now too, and directed by Yeon Sang-ho, the reliable mainstream genre man who made Train to Busan . If you’ve seen Na’s previous films and are looking for something more in line with them than this satire, try The Medium, which he co-wrote and produced. If you want to see a director at the height of his powers thumb his nose at Independence Day so he can piss off clueless consumers and executives, see Hope.

articles.title: Your memories of how you heard about 9/11 may well be wrong – we’ve been asking the same people what they remember for 25 years
articles.author:
<name>Elizabeth A. Phelps, Professor of Psychology, Harvard University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/elizabeth-a-phelps-2763358"/>
paras: How did you first learn of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001? Was it your mother’s panicked phone call? Your roommate shaking you awake with the news? The anxious chatter on your commuter train? No matter how you answer, our research suggests you may have around 40% of the details wrong.

The questions are not about the facts of the event itself, but rather the circumstance of learning about the event – what psychologists call flashbulb memories . People don’t remember such personal details for most news events, but for a select few, they do. For instance, Americans of a certain age also have flashbulb memories of hearing about President John F. Kennedy’s assassination.

Flashbulb memories can last a lifetime. Twenty-five years after the 9/11 attacks, people can still describe in detail how they learned of the attacks. But there is an important caveat: These long-lasting memories may not be as accurate as you might like to believe.

In research that we launched in the days after the attacks, we asked a few thousand people across the United States to tell us their memories . We asked them to tell us how they learned about the attacks, who they were with, where they were, what they were doing beforehand and how they felt. We also asked how confident they were that their memory was accurate.
We followed up with the same people one year, three years and 10 years later . We are now collecting their memories after a quarter century.

After only a year, about 40% of these details did not match what our volunteers had reported a few days after the attacks. Despite this high level of inconsistency, people were extremely confident their memories were correct.

For example, after a year, one person reported he was on the train when he heard of the attacks; initially he said he was at work. Another person initially described being with her husband; a year later she remembered being with her son.
Interestingly, these erroneous memories became stable over time. What most people reported after one year – even if the memory was in error – remained their memory when we assessed it later.

As you might imagine, when we talk about these findings, we are usually met with protest. People often tell us that this may be true of others, but they are certain their own memory is correct. We, too, believe our recollections of learning about 9/11 are accurate. But because we are memory researchers , we know there is a good chance that about 40% of the details we remember are wrong.
Psychologists have long known that memories are dynamic , not fixed .

Neuroscientists have uncovered windows of time when memories are vulnerable to change . That memories of 9/11 change over time is not surprising. Memory is a reconstruction of past events, not a stable archive. Errors are common . What is surprising is that people have a hard time believing their memories changed.

This incredulity is likely because people expect confidence in a memory’s accuracy to reflect its objective accuracy. Research shows that this assumption is generally true, but there are exceptions. Emotional events lead to both better memory for a few important details and greater confidence in that memory , despite worse recall for many other details .

And memories for emotional or important events are often discussed with others. Researchers have found that the social acknowledgment that accompanies sharing a memory can boost confidence in its accuracy . We believe that the inflated confidence we see for flashbulb memories of 9/11 emerges because the event was both highly emotional and people shared their experiences widely with others.
Being confident a memory is correct allows you to treat it as accurate, even if some details are not.

Memories you believe are accurate are more likely to shape your identity and guide your future actions. For significant personal events, people’s memories often shift to reflect themselves in the best possible light . People create a story of their life that enhances their well-being .

Being confident a memory is correct enables you to make it an important part of who you are. Flashbulb memories are specific to a community and help bind you to that community. For flashbulb memories of 9/11, this includes the social identity of being American.

A survey from the 1970s found 75% of Black Americans had flashbulb memories of learning of the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. , whereas only 32% of white Americans did. Most Britons have a flashbulb memory of learning of the death of Princess Diana . Most Italians do not.

Several studies underscore how flashbulb memories bind people together socially. One found that people perceived Americans who have a flashbulb memory of 9/11 to have a stronger American identity than those without a flashbulb memory. Another demonstrated that people think a person’s identity as an American would suffer if they lost their memory of 9/11 . This loss of identity was perceived as greater if the person forgot their flashbulb memory than if they forgot the attack itself.

So, if you told your story of how you learned about 9/11 on the recent anniversary, and if you tell it again in the future, you likely recounted a story you believe to be true, even if it is not completely accurate.

But getting a few details wrong may not be all that important. By telling your story, you are not just sharing an interesting tale with your companions. You are providing a narrative that binds you with other Americans, tacitly both asserting and affirming your shared membership in a community devastated by the terrorist attack that unfolded on Sept. 11, 2001.
Elizabeth A. Phelps receives funding from National Institutes of Health and the James S. McDonnell Foundation.
William Hirst has received funding from NIH, NSF, and the McDonnell Foundation.

articles.title: Seattle VR studio Polyarc, creator of ‘Moss’ series, closes down after almost 12 years
articles.author: Thomas Wilde
paras: The Seattle-based video game developer behind the award-winning virtual reality adventure Moss has closed its doors.
The announcement was made via Polyarc Games ’ LinkedIn page on Friday afternoon. No specific reason was offered for the studio’s closure.

“After nearly 12 years riding the joyous rollercoaster of emotions that is making video games, our time together has come to an end,” wrote an unnamed Polyarc representative. “Thank you to everyone at Polyarc. Our work is now finished.”

Twenty-nine employees will be dismissed due to the studio’s closure, including co-founders Chris Alderson, Danny Bulla, and CEO Tam Armstrong. Polyarc has posted a list of contact information and profiles for all affected employees, in an attempt to help them line up their next positions.

Polyarc’s first and best-known release was 2018’s Moss , where players helped guide a young mouse named Quill through a fantasy world on a journey to save her uncle. It was followed by 2022’s Moss: Book II , a direct sequel that continued Quill’s story, and the 2025 strategy spin-off Glassbreakers .
Polyarc’s most recent release was this year’s Moss: The Forgotten Relic for PC and console, which collected both Moss games into a single non-VR experience.

Armstrong, Bulla, and Alderson founded Polyarc as a startup in 2015 . All three were former employees of Bungie in Bellevue, where they’d all worked in different capacities on Bungie’s online shooter Destiny .

Polyarc’s closure comes almost six months after its announcement in March that it’d had to significantly reduce the size of the company, and almost eight months after a wave of layoffs at Meta that forced a major reduction at Bellevue, Wash.-based VR studio Camouflaj ( Republique, Batman: Arkham Shadow ).

As noted in January, Meta is perhaps the largest current player in the virtual reality sector, largely off the ubiquity of its standalone Quest headsets. When Meta decided to deemphasize its VR efforts in January, reportedly in favor of wearable computing and AI research , it touched off a negative ripple effect throughout the virtual reality field.

There is a chance that Valve’s upcoming Steam Frame may serve as an effective bailout for the VR sector by reigniting consumer interest, but at time of writing, the Frame has no release date. It’s apparently imminent, as suggested by a big leak in August , but there’s nothing definite. If the Steam Machine’s release in June was any indication, however, we can assume the Steam Frame will launch without warning on some random Tuesday morning in the next two months.

articles.title: Microsoft comms chief Frank Shaw to exit after nearly three decades shaping the company’s message
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: It’s the end of an era at Microsoft: Frank X. Shaw , the executive who oversaw the tech giant’s communications for nearly three decades, first at an external agency and for the last 17 years as one of its senior leaders, is leaving at the end of the year.
Shaw, 64, said he’s not retiring, although he doesn’t have another job lined up. He plans to stop working for a while, do some of the things he hasn’t had time for, and then decide what’s next.

“I have had a ringside seat at some of the biggest leadership, technology, and business transformations that have ever taken place,” Shaw said, sharing the news of his departure (under embargo) in a phone call Thursday afternoon. “I just feel incredibly fortunate.”
He said he had been discussing his potential departure for some time with Takeshi Numoto, Microsoft’s chief marketing officer, looking for the right moment.
Microsoft has not announced a successor for his role as chief communications officer. In a LinkedIn post , Shaw said the company will consider internal and external candidates.

A statement from Shaw’s colleagues in corporate communications credited him for his many years shaping Microsoft’s “voice and reputation with intelligence, candor and wit. His leadership and contributions to the company are too extensive to list, as is the number of journalists who have, at one point or another, used his name in vain.”

A former Marine Corps public affairs officer, Shaw has worked with all three of Microsoft’s CEOs. He started on the agency side, at Waggener Edstrom — now known as We. Communications — when Bill Gates was still running the company.

He built his reputation defending and advocating for Microsoft through some of its hardest stretches: the antitrust years, the Windows Vista backlash, the scramble to replace Steve Ballmer as CEO, and the weekend in 2023 when OpenAI’s board fired Sam Altman.

As the company’s top communications executive, he has also told the story of Microsoft’s reinvention under CEO Satya Nadella, from the LinkedIn and Activision Blizzard deals to an AI push that has carried Azure past $100 billion in annual revenue.
Evolving with technology: Shaw has spent much of his career closely watching the tech landscape and moving Microsoft’s voice into new channels as they emerged.

“We’re always thinking about what is the art and science of communications,” Shaw told PRWeek . “How do we reach our audiences most effectively in a changing environment?” He called the arc from print to radio and TV to social media and newsletters a “constant evolution of influence.”

He turned the corporate blog into a place where the company argued its own case, writing “Microsoft by the numbers” himself in 2010 — a stat-by-stat comparison against Apple and Google that TechCrunch dubbed “fantastic passive-aggressive.”

He and his team experimented with different and risky methods of telling the company’s story, holding mass briefings under embargo and publishing documents known as the “Book of News” in advance of its major keynotes and conferences. The prospect of a reporter having to answer to “fxs” was no doubt a factor in ensuring the news (mostly) didn’t leak.

Shaw hired Steve Clayton out of a technical role at Microsoft in London, where he had been blogging about the company unofficially out of frustration with how it was perceived, and made him chief storyteller. In the middle of the AI boom, Clayton and Shaw embraced the analog undercurrents in popular culture and launched Signal , a quarterly Microsoft print magazine for business leaders.

Clayton was VP of communications strategy by the time he left in January to become chief communications officer at Cisco, making Shaw’s planned departure the second high-profile exit from Microsoft’s comms team in a year.

Adapting to AI: In recent years, Shaw made his own team a testing ground for AI, publishing what worked and what didn’t. In a 2023 post he described using Copilot in Teams to pull story ideas out of conversations with spokespeople and anticipate coverage after interviews, and asking the AI to “poke holes in a statement we’re making on a tricky topic.”

He called it his corporal, a reference to Napoleon, who was said to bring one to meetings and ask whether his generals’ war plans made sense to him. A survey of 80 people in Microsoft’s communications and marketing organization found 84% did not want to go back to working without it.
Shaw was also known to use AI as a sounding board when a story frustrated him, offering him an objective take before he called and let a particular reporter have it.
He announced his departure Friday morning in a message to Microsoft’s communications team (reminding them he’s still there for a few months yet) and his public post on LinkedIn.

“Thank you as well to all the reporters, editors, writers, influencers and analysts who have put up with me over this time, enduring my early and late night calls, my off the record ‘no comments,’ my bad story ideas and my extended commentary on headlines and positioning,” he wrote.
“You all have incredibly hard and valuable jobs,” he added, “and while I’ve not agreed with everything said about us 😊 I appreciate you anyway.”

articles.title: From OK grades to Dartmouth Hall of Fame: Remitly’s Matt Oppenheimer on his ‘strengths and shadows’
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Nearly 25 years after enrolling at Dartmouth College to study psychology and embarking on a path that led him to co-found Seattle fintech giant Remitly, Matt Oppenheimer has been inducted into the Ivy League school’s Entrepreneur Hall of Fame.

The honor, presented Thursday night in San Francisco as part of Dartmouth’s annual Entrepreneurs Forum, comes seven months after Oppenheimer stepped down as Remitly’s long-time CEO to become chairman of the board.

Created by the Magnuson Center for Entrepreneurship , the Hall of Fame honors Dartmouth alumni who have made lasting positive impacts through their ventures. Oppenheimer joins a select group of honorees with Northwest ties — including Smartsheet co-founders Brent Frei and Mark Mader — and used his acceptance remarks to express deep gratitude to the admissions officers who took a chance on a kid from Boise, Idaho, with “OK grades” and “below average SAT scores.”
Speaking with GeekWire ahead of the event, Oppenheimer recalled how his early college years studying social psychology helped shape his understanding of business.

“I think a lot of business and entrepreneurship does come down to interpersonal dynamics,” Oppenheimer said. “I am a people person. But how do you find what I call career-market fit when it comes to really understanding and connecting with people? That’s ultimately my strength, but it was really hard to define earlier in my career.”

After graduating from Dartmouth in 2005, Oppenheimer earned an MBA from Harvard Business School and worked in Kenya for Barclays Bank, where seeing families hit with steep fees on cross-border money transfers inspired him to start Remitly in 2011.

He served as CEO for nearly 15 years, guiding the company through its 2021 NASDAQ IPO and building it into a fintech powerhouse serving over 9 million customers across more than 170 countries before transitioning to chairman in February.
In his acceptance speech on Thursday, Oppenheimer focused on a central philosophy he calls leading authentically through “towering strengths and shadows.”

“Each of us has a few towering strengths — things we are in the top 10% of the world at doing. Not good at. Towering,” he said. “And almost always, that tower casts a shadow. The same trait that makes you exceptional at one thing quietly makes you a liability at another. They aren’t two traits. They’re one trait, seen from two sides.”
He pointed to his own extreme tenacity as an example, noting how it helped him build Remitly through years of investor rejections and early product stumbles, but how it also had a darker side.

“That same tenacity can lock onto things that are unhealthy, or unchangeable, or both,” Oppenheimer shared, candidly discussing his personal experiences with OCD-related anxiety and depression. “This isn’t a character flaw sitting next to my strengths. It is the shadow of my greatest strength, from the same place. Which means it’s something to work with … harness the tower, manage the shadow … rather than something to be ashamed of.”

Seven months into his transition from operational CEO to board chairman, Oppenheimer says the shift has felt surprisingly comfortable. Free from managing daily execution, he now channels that same intensity into coaching current leaders and serving on corporate boards.

“I have so much trust in Sebastian [Gunningham], our CEO, and it’s super exciting to support him in a chair capacity,” Oppenheimer told GeekWire. “I get to share reflections on the journey, mentor, and coach. I didn’t know that would be the case, because you hear so many examples of founder-CEOs who transition and have a really hard time with it.”

That mentorship extends to Seattle’s broader startup community, where Oppenheimer is an active member of Foundations, a collective of local tech founders and AI leaders. When advising early stage entrepreneurs, he urges them to remain hyper-focused on solving a single, deep customer problem rather than spreading themselves thin.
And while AI has vastly accelerated product development, Oppenheimer notes that the core fundamentals of building a business haven’t changed.

“With fintech, you still have to build the trust, get the licensing, and build out the compliance infrastructure and banking relationships,” he said. “The actual building and deployment of product got a lot faster, but if you don’t have great judgment, you can go down the wrong path pretty quickly.”

Looking back 25 years later, Oppenheimer noted that the Dartmouth admissions officers who took a chance on him didn’t look past his test scores by accident — they told him years later that they were drawn to his personal qualities and humanity.

“Two strangers in an office in Hanover found my tower before I had any idea what it was, and then they handed me the place to build on it,” Oppenheimer said in his closing remarks. “That isn’t a debt. It’s a privilege. And the only sensible thing to do with a privilege is use it well.”

articles.title: Raiders star Ashton Jeanty backs Nukleus, a tech platform for athletes and their advisors
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Hector Rivas spent a decade building ThriftBooks into one of the country’s largest used-book sellers, before an unlikely second act: co-founding a sports agency representing NFL players.
That career change led him to the problem behind his newest startup, and to the Las Vegas Raiders running back who just invested in it.

Nukleus , based in Issaquah, Wash., is building what Rivas calls an operating system for the business of sports. The idea is a single workspace for everyone in an athlete’s orbit: agent, lawyer, CPA, financial advisor, marketing team, and others. It lets them all work from the same contracts, deadlines and records, rather than each keeping a separate pile of emails and spreadsheets.
The idea came out of Rivas’s years at Disruptive Sports, the agency he co-founded in 2020 and left earlier this year.
Ashton Jeanty , who signed a four-year, $35.9 million rookie contract with the Raiders in 2025, has taken equity in the company and signed on to serve as its public face.

Nukleus has also named four strategic investors: Mat McBride , Microsoft’s executive vice president and CFO for commercial products and infrastructure; WaFd Bank President and CEO Brent Beardall ; investor Skyler Nelson , previously of Vulcan Capital and its successor firm Cercano; and Dr. Brett Kindle of the Andrews Institute in Gulf Breeze, Fla.
The company has a team of 12 based out of its Issaquah office, plus a supporting engineering team in India. Most of the team is engineering.

Other executives include CTO Eric Ahlstrom , previously at Microsoft, Unity, Oracle and ESPN; chief creative officer Ben Miller , a former creative director at the University of Washington and CAA Sports; and CFO Matt Porter , who worked with Rivas at ThriftBooks, EcoGoodz and Disruptive.
Nukleus closed a pre-seed round from friends and family in 2025 and is raising again now. Rivas declined to disclose the amount raised by the company so far.

From books to football: Rivas was ThriftBooks’ first CEO, running the used-book seller for about a decade after it launched in 2003. Based in the Seattle area, the company grew during his tenure from a storage unit in Kirkland, Wash., to 10 distribution facilities in 10 states, by his account.
He went on to found EcoGoodz, a used-goods and overstock brokerage, and in 2020 co-founded Disruptive Sports Agency with agent Henry Organ.
Rivas, an NFLPA-certified contract advisor, worked the business side of the agency. He left earlier this year to build Nukleus full time.
The years inside the agency are what produced the idea.

Everyone in a player’s orbit was working off “their own version of the truth,” Rivas explained via email: the agent, the lawyer, the CPA, the financial advisor, the marketing team. The athlete, he said, “was the one absorbing the cost of that disconnect,” in slower decisions and deals that fell through the cracks.
The pitch in Las Vegas: Jeanty and Rivas knew each other from Rivas’s years at the sports agency, and Rivas said the running back had been tracking what he was building.
“Because Ashton and I already knew each other, and he’d been aware of what I was building, the conversation came together naturally,” Rivas said.
He flew to Las Vegas to walk Jeanty through the model, the team, and where the company was headed. Rivas said Jeanty’s equity reflects both money invested and his role promoting the platform.
In a statement, Jeanty described the job of running his own career.

“Coming into the NFL, you become a CEO, directing a team of agents, advisors, and marketers, whether you’re ready or not,” he said. “Nukleus is what finally gets them all on the same page, so I can actually run that team the way it should be run. That’s why I invested in it.”

Where things stand: The product is in a free beta with about 30 users, including athletes, agents, agencies, lawyers and marketing staff. Nukleus plans to charge $99 per user per month for a starter plan and $249 for a full-featured one, with custom enterprise pricing. Athletes join free.
Alongside contract storage, deadline tracking and a shared workspace, the company is building AI tools meant to answer questions about contract terms and league rules.

Others are working similar territory. Agent Live 360 sells software built specifically for sports agents, and Opendorse , which says it works with more than 1,000 sports agents, offers tools to negotiate, approve and track deals. Nukleus says it differs from narrower tools by serving everyone in an athlete’s orbit.
The bigger bet: The company is looking well past a single app.

“Long-term, I don’t see this as a tool athletes use, I see it as the infrastructure the entire business of sports runs on,” Rivas said. “Every athlete becomes the center of their own connected team, and every professional working with them, across every sport, at every level, operates on one shared system instead of a hundred disconnected ones.”

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: New Speed Cameras
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On Wednesday, SDOT announced four new speed cameras will be installed across Seattle in 2027. These four cameras are the first of 10 cameras that will be installed by March 2029, per Mayor Wilson’s Vision Zero executive order . The selected locations were chosen as they are some of the most dangerous sections of Seattle’s road network. Speed cameras cannot replace full road redesigns, but they are an effective temporary measure until a concrete redesign is implemented. The four cameras will be installed at:

These broad sections will be narrowed down to the exact camera locations over the next few months. Signs warning drivers of the cameras will be installed 30 days before the cameras are turned on. Once the cameras are enabled, they will only issue warnings for the first 30 days.

The four locations chosen for this initial batch of speed cameras are hotspots for dangerous driving. SDOT data show these sections have an 85th percentile speed more than 10mph above the speed limit. While a 5mph or 10mph difference may be insignificant to a driver, faster speeds are much more deadly. A 2011 study found that someone has a 70% higher chance of being killed by a vehicle traveling at 30mph versus at 25mph. Over the last three years, the four sections have collectively had 305 crashes that caused 138 injuries and 3 fatalities.

The four new cameras will join a growing network of red light cameras, school speed safety cameras, block the box cameras, and bus lane cameras. These cameras are not used for any purposes other than traffic safety. From SDOT: “State law requires that traffic safety cameras may only film when they detect a traffic violation. The video cannot be used as evidence to prosecute other kinds of crimes aside from speeding.”

articles.title: Faulty Pantograph Blamed for Sound Transit's Apple Cup Train Stall
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Sound Transit has blamed a "misaligned pantograph" – the steel arm that draws power from overhead wire – for causing a "voltage spike" that stalled a crowded 2 Line train for several hours on Sunday evening.

Following a heavily attended Apple Cup college football game at Husky Stadium, a packed train headed north from the University District stalled in the tunnel south of Roosevelt Station, causing a service disruption that lasted more than two hours. Riders reported that lighting and air conditioning went out intermittently on the stalled train, which was crammed full of rowdy college football fans leaving a Huskies victory.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

With an uncomfortable wait of undetermined length, some opened train doors and poured into the tunnel to get a little breathing room and cooler air. Confusion abounded onboard the stalled train and at stations up and down the line as the blockage forced delays that rippled across the system.
Sound Transit spokesperson Henry Bendon said the agency swept into action to deploy rescue trains and mobilize staff to direct riders to buses or alternate means of transport.

"On Sunday evening at about 5:50, a northbound 2 Line train experienced a mechanical issue and became stranded between U District and Roosevelt stations," Bendon told The Urbanist . "We deployed rescue trains to retrieve passengers from the disabled train, and our fare ambassadors and security staff directed passengers to alternate bus service. Normal operations resumed at about 8:20 p.m."
For some, Metro bus service was not a viable replacement for light rail, forcing them to utilize other options, like ridehailing.
Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine promised an investigation and a full report back to the agency's board of directors at a System Expansion committee briefing on Thursday afternoon.

"A full investigation into the root cause is underway, but it appears to be related to the pantograph, the arm that extends from the train's roof that draws power from the overhead line," Constantine said. "Our maintenance team found that it was misaligned and causing a voltage spike. The pantograph has, of course, been repaired and successfully tested on the mainline."

Sunday's snafu adds another blemish on a rocky two-month span with fairly frequent light rail service disruptions, many of an unplanned nature. The highest profile was a train derailment on August 1, though mechanical issues and a power outage caused three separate disruptions in July, after a miraculous disruption-free FIFA Men's World Cup.

It also marked the second time such a train stall has occurred during the Apple Cup, when the University of Washington Huskies football team squares off with the Washington State Cougars. The last Apple Cup hiccup was in 2021, though that incident had a different cause, and occurred shortly after Sound Transit opened the segment of the 1 Line between University of Washington station and Northgate.

"The problem appears entirely different from the 2021 Apple Cup stall, when the weight of a packed train caused it to squat lower than usual , and a power cable on the train’s underside was sliced by protruding bolts on the tunnel floor, near UW Station," Seattle Times' Mike Lindblom reported Thursday. "Those were identified by front-line workers earlier in the year but didn’t get trimmed down, a Sound Transit investigation revealed."

Lindblom noted that members of the agency’s Citizen Oversight Panel were not pleased about how the incident was communicated to riders, and they shared their frustration with CEO Dow Constantine at the panel's online meeting Wednesday.

"The panel’s chair, Charlotte Murry of Snohomish County, said she was aboard a stopped train, despite having waited an hour after the football game in hopes crowds were thinning out," Lindlom wrote. "She used the word 'unprofessional' to describe what seemed like a disorganized response."

Sound Transit said when disruptions occur, the agency prioritizes swift restoration of service and prompt rider communications. Sunday's chaos shows the message might not always be getting through clearly on the ground to exasperated riders.

"We know this was a major inconvenience and stressful situation for our passengers," Bendon said in an email. "Our focus remains on proactively minimizing the risk of disruptions. When they do occur, we work to respond and restore service as quickly as possible. We also prioritize rider communications during disruptions and incident response, including digital alerts, in-station messaging, and in-person support from staff and contracted security."
Constantine echoed that sentiment and pledged to report back to the board for an in-depth look at passenger communications and responsiveness to service disruptions.

"We understand how frustrating this type of disruption can be to our passengers, and I have ordered full internal review of the incident, including a focus on understanding our passenger communications and our overall agency responsiveness, and I plan to bring those findings back to this committee or to the board for an in-depth discussion."
Even before this latest incident, many observers (including Sound Transit board member Claudia Balducci) had called on the agency to fine tune its approach to rider communications during disruptions.

articles.title: New Airo Trains Start Rolling on Amtrak Cascades September 30
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Train riders getting around the Pacific Northwest now have less than three weeks to wait for brand new trainsets complete with new ergonomic seats, upgraded WiFi, and a revamped cafe car. On Thursday, the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) revealed that two "Airo" trainsets will start operating on Wednesday, September 30 on the Amtrak Cascades corridor.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!
September 30 also happens to be when Sound Transit is inaugurating service on Pinehurst Station , an infill light rail stop between Northgate and South Shoreline.

The Airos, which are being manufactured by Siemens, were ordered in 2021 and will replace aging equipment on the Cascades corridor. While no additional roundtrips are planned with the new sets compared to the existing Amtrak Cascades schedule, each Airo will have much more seating capacity: 317 seats compared to as few as 160 seats that are available on the Amfleet I cars in most common use otherwise.

Amtrak Cascades, which is jointly sponsored by WSDOT and the Oregon Department of Transportation, will be the first regional Amtrak route to see the new Airo trains before they get rolled out elsewhere in the U.S. The exact trips that will see Airos put in place has not yet been announced.

The announcement of a firm date came at a meeting of the Puget Sound Regional Council's transportation policy board, after months of sightings of the Airo trains around the region following the arrival of the first set on May 16 and the second on August 23. Amtrak took possession of the first two Airo trainsets in February, putting them through the paces through cross-country testing after a public unveiling at Union Station in Washington, D.C.
The third trainset arrived in Seattle today, according to WSDOT Freight and Rail Planning Program Manager Jason Beloso.

The Airo trains will come with a bevy of new upgrades, including bathrooms with touchless controls for better sanitation, seating with large tray tables, water bottle holders, and cushioned headrests, and coaches with more reliable WiFi and enhanced lighting systems. The sleeker cafe cars will offer a Northwest-themed food and beverage menu.

Beloso said Thursday that the initial launch this month will include one new trainset on the Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. route, and another on the Seattle to Eugene route, with a third set kept on hand as a spare. The additional five trainsets are expected to arrive before the end of the year, part of a larger, nationwide order of 83 trainsets.

When fully in operation, the new fleet of Airos will significantly boost the capacity on the Amtrak Cascades network, especially the overprescribed Vancouver, B.C. route which regularly sells out weeks in advance.

Amtrak will be well-prepared for an influx of visitors heading from Canada, after rolling out a first-on-the-continent rail travel preclearance facility at Vancouver's Pacific Central Station earlier this year. That facility allows southbound trains to cross the border without stopping for any additional screening.

Ridership on Amtrak Cascades had been steadily increasing in recent years, but hit a wall when Amtrak was forced to swap out 26 railcars on the corridor for smaller vehicles in 2025, after discovering potential issues with its previously used Talgo trainsets. Replacing the Talgos with Amfleet I vehicles from elsewhere in the country reduced capacity on the entire Cascades system, leading to an 8% drop in ridership between 2024 and 2025.
That being said, the entire Amtrak system saw a boost in usage for the FIFA Men's World Cup, with the system carrying a record five million riders in the weeks surrounding the matches.
With the new Airo fleet, the upper limit on ridership potential for Amtrak Cascades will be substantially raised.

Amtrak is also making steady progress on its revamped Seattle trainyard , a $300 million project funded by the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act . Unlike previous generations of Amtrak trainsets, the Airos aren't able to be decoupled, prompting the need for a much larger maintenance facility. The structure taking shape right now in SoDo certainly fits that bill, coming in at 100,000 square feet.

The City of Seattle is also working with Amtrak on another major headache for rail operations in the city: the at-grade crossing at S Holgate Street that is essentially the only public road running directly through a rail maintenance facility anywhere in the U.S. A new study is looking at ways to address the inherent conflicts at that location, including with a potential full closure and/or pedestrian and vehicle bridge. Improving that pinch point could allow the Seattle railyard to handle even more trains down the line.

Amtrak is also working on a $110 million retrofit of the rail bridge over Salmon Bay between Ballard and Magnolia, a key segment of the Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. route. That upgrade is expected to extend the life of the bridge by 50 years. Another $12 million in landslide mitigation efforts and $12.9 in trackside equipment improvements are also on deck.

The infrastructure improvements are nice, but the real star of the show will be the new trainsets. With the Airos finally going into service, the next generation of Amtrak service is definitely at Seattle's doorstep, a fact that is sure to bring some major benefits for regional travel throughout the Pacific Northwest.

articles.title: Microsoft, Starbucks, and biz leaders demand 100-day Seattle ‘public safety action plan’ as budget fight looms
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A coalition of 38 regional business leaders delivered a letter Thursday urging Mayor Katie Wilson and Seattle City Council president and District 3 representative Joy Hollingsworth to adopt an immediate “100-day public safety action plan” with “concrete” performance metrics, arriving just ahead of fall city budget negotiations.

Organized by the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce , “CEO-level civic alliance” Challenge Seattle , and the statewide lobbyist Washington Roundtable , the letter is signed by executives including Microsoft’s Brad Smith, Starbucks’ Brian Niccol, Costco’s Ron Vachris, and Alaska Airlines’ Ben Minicucci . The signatories asserted that “voters are asking for action, on a timeline, with results they can measure,” citing an August Chamber survey where only 34% of 500 registered voters expressed confidence in Seattle’s public safety approach, while they say 86% backed a 100-day framework.

“The clearest message from our August 17 joint public-opinion poll of registered Seattle voters is this: residents expect the City to act with urgency, fund the actions needed to improve safety, and provide a clear plan for measuring progress,” the letter (PDF) reads.

The demands establish benchmarks including requiring a 7-minute 911 response target and reporting missed calls, noting police responded to only 29% of calls at Nordstrom’s downtown flagship compared to 100% at its Bellevue and Southcenter stores. Reactivating CCTV networks in Pioneer Square and the Stadium District (75% voter support), deploying walking and bike beats (90% support), and clearing encampments within 250 feet of parks and schools within 72 hours (79% support) are also part of the call.

The group also warned against cutting police funding, stating Seattle’s 1.31 sworn officers per 1,000 residents is “about 40% fewer than Denver, 43% fewer than San Francisco and 58% fewer than Boston.”

The sudden corporate urgency arrives against the backdrop of an intensifying tax fight. As a former Transit Riders Union organizer, Wilson helped architect the city’s JumpStart payroll tax on big business, and she enters her first budget cycle facing a projected deficit while evaluating expanded progressive revenue options, including levies on major employers and top earners. Framing the city’s challenges around basic public safety delivery and lagging response times provides large corporate interests potent leverage to oppose new tax proposals, pushing City Hall to prioritize policing over progressive revenue policies.
The mayor’s office hasn’t exactly presented a strong front on responding to public safety concerns, focusing instead of replacing the police chief and prioritizing police alternatives.

The Wilson administration’s public safety stances have championed civilian alternatives, harm reduction, and supportive housing over traditional police expansion and misdemeanor prosecution. In policy, Wilson has focused on administrative accountability and targeted street deployments. After the July Seattle Center shooting, she forced the resignation of Chief Shon Barnes , appointed Interim Chief Andre Sayles , and instituted a one-hour public notification target for major incidents. Her administration has also directed increased police patrols and environmental modifications to persistent hotspots like Belltown, Little Saigon, and North Aurora, while putting SPD’s Real Time Crime Center camera expansion on hold.
Her strongest public safety actions have been the new public safety communication practices and the launch of a nationwide search for a new Seattle police chief.

Capitol Hill and the Central District representative and current president of the council Hollingsworth, meanwhile, has approached public safety through a centrist “both/and” lens, trying to balance support for traditional law enforcement with community-based intervention and civilian alternatives. While she advocates for stronger police staffing and visible foot beats in commercial corridors like Pike/Pine, she has championed the civilian CARE department to divert nonviolent mental health calls away from armed officers. In a break with the mayor, Hollingsworth has helped lead the council majority in supporting legal deterrence mechanisms, including Stay Out of Drug Areas zones to disrupt chronic open-air illicit markets.

Hollingsworth has also championed economics in the public safety debate, treating small business stability as an essential component of public safety and backing initiatives like the proposed Pike/Pine Business Improvement Area to fund localized safety and sanitation resources.

The council president has also taken a broader approach to gun violence with support for community intervention including funding for organizations like Community Passageways that provide on-the-ground support at Garfield High School .
Meanwhile, the council’s public safety chair Bob Kettle has lately focused his energy on Wilson’s decision to push Barnes out.
President Hollingsworth has not yet publicly responded to the chamber’s call for a safety plan.

Responding to the letter, Wilson said the city is “making progress, step by step,” noting that while homicides and shootings sit at decade lows, “we have far too much crime and public disorder, and people have a right to be frustrated.”

Headed into her first budget battle on the mayor’s side of the desk, Wilson may need to provide a larger, more expensive response to that frustration. Many of the same issues listed in the chamber’s letter were raised in an East Precinct community crime meeting held by SPD at Capitol HIll’s Miller Community Center Wednesday night. There were no CEOs or leaders from the region’s biggest companies in attendance.

articles.title: TikTok Made 9/11 a Catastrophe Among So Many Catastrophes
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: “Shame on them for doing that!” a white boomer said to me as I stood near the corner of Minor Avenue and Virginia Street looking at the tail of the decommissioned 747 that’s between two luxury towers in the Denny Triangle. She wore sunglasses and a coat too thick for the hot July afternoon. She was also pushing a pram with a small dog in it. “Think of the people who died in 9/11. It’s so disrespectful to them. How could they do this? A plane crashing into the buildings. It’s just unthinkable. And I have to look at it every day.”

I didn’t make the connection between the 747, which, when completed, might become a bar or music venue, and 9/11. I said to her, “But that happened way, way up there; this plane is very close to the ground.” She looked at me with suspicion and said, “Well, the planes fell to the ground, didn’t they?” I suppose so, I thought. Now she was pissed at me and the developers of Aero1200 ’s skyscrapers. Her dog, who looked like an Ewok , could tell I had upset their companion. I turned my back to both of them and crossed the street to have a closer look at the plane’s tail.

The truth of the matter is I’ve never had powerful feelings about 9/11, in part because I place nationalism in the same category as “village feeling.” which, as the Japanese philosopher Kojin Karatani put it in The Structure of World History , has its raison d’etre in xenophobia: the fear of strangers, of outsiders. Village feeling is the soil on which fascism can only grow. This is why so much noise has been made on the right about the mayor of New York City, Zohran Kwame Mamdani, attending the “ 9/11 remembrance at Ground Zero .” He is a Muslim and therefore a stranger and outsider. Those who destroyed the towers were strangers, outsiders, Muslims. The ideal person to lead an event that tightens, deepens, strengthens village feelings of this kind has to be white, male, hetero, and Christian.

As a foreign-born American (Black, African, agnostic), nationalism is a dead end because by its very nature it can’t be inclusive. This is why the patriotism of the left is always questioned, doubted, and distrusted: our political position is inherently cosmopolitan. Nationalism can only truly be the domain of the right because it demands that one (white, male, Christian) type not only be the default but also subordinate all others. Mamdani is not that type. Nor am I.

But what to make of the terrorist action that took place 25 years ago in Manhattan if submission to the village feeling is not an option? For this other kind of feeling, and one I feel powerfully, we must turn to Walter Benjamin, a great 20th century critical theorist who, being a Jewish intellectual, committed suicide in 1940 after failing to flee the Nazis.

In his posthumously published masterpiece, “ Theses on the Concept of History, ” he presents the Angle of History. Benjamin writes in these IX: “This is how one pictures the angel of history. His face is turned toward the past. Where we perceive a chain of events, he sees one single catastrophe which keeps piling wreckage and hurls it in front of his feet.”

The catastrophe was there before 9/11; and it didn’t stop after 9/11: the Iraq War, the Afghanistan War, the Mumbai Attacks, the Norway attack, October 7, the destruction of Gaza and of Lebanon, the bombing of schoolgirls in Iran. Wreckage upon wreckage being hurled to the feet of history’s angel. This, I have been told by a number of Gen Zers, is exactly why they can’t fully appreciate the singularity of 9/11. The destruction they’ve seen on social media platforms such as TikTok has made 9/11 one among many catastrophes that have happened between then (when they were born) and now (the US is again at war in the Middle East).

Benjamin concludes thesis IX on this pessimistic note: “The angel would like to… awaken the dead, and make whole what has been smashed. But a storm is blowing in from Paradise; it has got caught in his wings with such a violence that the angel can no longer close them.”
