articles.title: Six Questions for Matt Midgley on What it’s Like to Run an Art Gallery in Pike Place
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: Buried below the flying fish and banjo-plucking buskers at Pike Place Market, you’ll find Gallery ERGO , a contemporary art gallery that celebrates its fifth anniversary today.

What began as a shared artist studio in 2019 gradually shifted into a place for selling artists’ work, and eventually into a full-blown gallery operated and curated by Matt Midgley, who took over the space with his wife, Elaine Saly, to rescue it from obsolescence. Midgley is an accomplished artist in his own right: His acid-trippy, Escher-esque Op-Art confections are delicious to look at. Saly, a public defender and avid art lover, is his partner in the enterprise.

Because it’s in the market, ERGO has a slightly different feel from most galleries—no ivory tower, it’s down and dirty in the busy mix of crowds and vendors. It’s also unusual because it’s run by an artist: Midgley brings an artist’s eye and his personal network into the curatorial conversation, drawing artists from around the world to this sweet little spot tucked in a tourist maze. The work he curates has range, but you can count on encountering paintings and drawings with extreme, lush color and technical precision, leaning into street art, pop-surrealist-tinged painting, and hyperrealism, with some photography and sculpture as well. (ERGO is where I first encountered KSRA’s jaw-dropping miniatures .)

Today, ERGO is celebrating its five-year anniversary with a giant group show that features new work by more than 40 of its favorite artists, alongside a solo show of work by Berlin-based artist SNYDER . (The reception runs from 5-8 p.m., no RSVP necessary.) We asked Midgley a few questions about how he, an accidental gallerist, even got here.

You didn’t wake up one day and decide you’re going to be a gallery owner. How did you get here—what’s the ERGO lore? MIDGLEY: Opening a gallery was never something I had plans to do or even imagined I would be doing. The day I decided to do it was, I believe, the same day the thought first entered my mind. I had joined a co-op artist studio space that my friend (and rad artist) Ariel Parrow was running in a shop space at Pike Place Market. I had just quit my previous day job, hoping to find something better for my happiness and general mental health. I decided to take what very small savings I had and pretend I was a full-time artist for a couple months before finding another job. Then, an opportunity came to me to take over the space, and the idea to make the shift from a studio space to a gallery was born.

You have a pretty distinct eye and taste. How do you know when something belongs at ERGO? MIDGLEY: There isn’t really a set rubric or system, I just know what I like and what I find interesting or exciting! That changes over time, too, of course. I definitely have a fondness for artists who have really dialed in their particular approach.

Do you think of yourself as an artist who runs a gallery, or have you become a gallery owner who happens to be an artist? Is there a difference? MIDGLEY: Between those two options—and based on my output over the last few years—I think it would land me squarely in the gallery-owner-who-happens-to-be-an-artist camp, but I don’t think the two really need to be ordered necessarily. I consider myself an artist and curator/gallery owner.

What’s the strangest conversation you’ve overheard in the gallery? MIDGLEY: There’s so many people at Pike Place Market, you catch a snippet of something hilarious, curious, and/or insane pretty regularly. One thing I’ve noticed is how many people who frequent the market genuinely believe it to be haunted at night. Though that kind of thing I suppose just comes with the territory on a 119-year-old building!
Have you seen a ghost there? MIDGLEY: I have not. I feel like believing in ghosts is probably a key factor in supposedly seeing them, and I don’t.

What’s one piece of advice about the art business you think is total bullshit? MIDGLEY: I’m not sure it counts as advice, but I think the idea that you aren’t really a professional artist unless you’re doing it full time and living off it is totally bullshit. If you are lucky enough to get to focus on the arts and that’s working out for you enough to cover your bills, that’s awesome! But that’s just one path, and an unfortunately unlikely one for most of us. If you make art, you’re an artist.

What’s more, if you can find a day job that you don’t hate and that gives you some free time to make art without the need for that art to also pay your rent, sometimes that’s actually the better path. You can create without the stress associated with need for sales, and focus on things you really want to see out there in the world, regardless of whether there’s financial return on that investment. In my experience, some of the happiest working artists go this route.

What’s something you’ve learned about people by watching them look at art? MIDGLEY: In my opinion, whether people know it or not, we’re all hungry for art that does something to us. Something that moves us, something that challenges us, something that makes us feel something. And people often seem surprised at which art does that to them! I think that, in this way, we learn new things about ourselves in the process.

articles.title: Slog AM: Businesses Send Angry Letter to Seattle Mayor, McClatchy Slits Local Journalism’s Throat, and It’s 9/11
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: 25 years since, well, you know: It’s 9/11. People are gathering across the country to mourn and commemorate the day. President Donald Trump is speaking at the Pentagon. Oddly, he’s not going to New York where everything went down. He sent his vassal, Vice President J.D. Vance. Former Presidents George W. Bush, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, Joe Biden also attended the New York memorial .

An imperfect way to commemorate 9/11: United Airlines planned a flyover of Denver to commemorate 9/11. They wanted to send a United Boeing 777 accompanied by fighter jets low over Denver as “a meaningful gesture to honor the memory of those lost within the pilot community.” United canceled its flyover after hearing concerns from the community because, well, you know.

Never forget the SEA Spot Saver program. The sanctioned TSA line-cutting system at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport i s going the way of the dodo bird on November 30. Sea-Tac said, with new security checkpoints opening, it has outgrown the need for Spot Saver.
Strike on the horizon: More than 300 Shoreline School District staff could strike starting Monday if the union and district don’t reach a contract agreement by Sunday.

Oh no, the big businesses are mad: Business leaders from 38 companies, including Starbucks, Microsoft, Costco, Nordstrom, the Seattle Mariners, and Alaska Air Group, sent a strongly-worded letter urging Mayor Katie Wilson and the Seattle City Council to create a 100-day public safety action plan. The letter is in response to an August poll , conducted by our town’s business circle jerk, the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, that found where only 34 percent of 500 registered Seattle voters were confident in the city’s public safety plan. Well, boo hoo. Violent crime is down through the first half of 2026. Where was this angry letter to the last two mayors, when violent crime rates were much higher ?

Three of these companies aren’t even based in this city and one is in the process of relocating a bunch of jobs to Nashville. They do not care about this city; they care about power and influence, something they do not have over Katie Wilson. Which—not sure if I have to spell it out—is a good thing.

McClatchy bloodbath: Hedge fund-owned McClatchy laid off more than 90 journalists on Thursday at 13 of its 30 papers across eight states. In the Northwest, McClatchy laid off 33 percent of unionized workers at the Idaho Statesman , The News Tribune (Tacoma), Tri-City Herald , The Olympian, and Bellingham Herald . McClatchy explained the layoffs as a response to “changing subscriber interests and the ways audiences engage with local news.” The bloodsuckers are “refocusing resources on journalism that subscribers value.” I guess that means cutting Miami and Miami Beach beats at The Miami Herald .
The weather: The clouds are back. Rain will come this weekend. Rejoice.

A perfect way to commemorate 9/11: The price of oil jumped to $110 a barrel and US diesel is going for $6 a gallon. The escalating war with Iran is not helping things, in fact, it is driving this. The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have taken full control of the Red Sea coastline, where another vital global shipping route, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, is located. Rising prices at the pump should spell midterm doom for Trump. He must have an inkling of this, since, in a rambling speech, he beseeched the crowd at the Republican National Convention to “get out and vote, and you’re going to pretend I’m on the ballot. Because in a way, I’m on the ballot.”

Claude, make me a biological weapon to destroy all humans, please: Anthropic released a new report that detailed misuses of its Claude AI chatbot including multiple instances of scientists using it for research that could create new biological weapons . Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research was for “legitimate or nefarious reasons,” since this work could be used for vaccine development, and shut down those projects. In one instance, a scientist on a military base used Claude to engineer mutations of chikungunya virus, a mosquito-born illness that causes intense pain, to make it even more painful. Anthropic shut that down. Perhaps we should heed the researchers who are banging the “ AI could kill us all ” drum. Supervillain stuff!

Ectopic pregnancy deaths on the rise: An ectopic pregnancy occurs when an embryo implants somewhere other than the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube. As the embryo grows, the organ will rupture, which can be fatal if untreated. The treatment is abortion. In recent years—since the COVID-19 pandemic and since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade —ectopic pregnancy deaths have nearly doubled—between 2020 and 2025 almost 200 women died from ectopic pregnancies, reports ProPublica . In the previous six years, 100 women died. The phenomenon is not limited to states with abortion bans, but it is certainly more common anywhere doctors refuse to act or wait in fear of breaking state law.
“Costa Rican man, 119, seeks recognition as world’s oldest person.” Alright, yeah, man. Here you go . You can have it.
ICYMI: Capitol Hill’s closed Egyptian theater may rise again. This time it won’t be operated by SIFF. Charles Mudede has the scoop .

articles.title: The Best New Restaurants in the Seattle Area
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: The Eater Seattle Heatmap aims to answer the question “Where should I eat right now?” for people trying to keep up with the city’s constantly changing dining landscape. It focuses on newer restaurants — typically opened or revamped significantly within the last six months or so — that are reshaping Seattle’s food scene for the better.

articles.title: How anti-bribery laws apply to Trump’s promise of $5,000 payments if Republicans keep control of Congress
articles.author:
<name>Austin Sarat, William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science, Amherst College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/austin-sarat-174772"/>
paras: In his keynote address to the Republican midterm convention on Sept. 9, 2026, President Donald Trump promised that if Republicans retain control of Congress in November, he would authorize a US$5,000 payment to every American adult .
Trump’s offer seems to run afoul of federal laws, which make it a crime to pay for votes .
After Trump’s speech, political commentator Sam Stein posted on X: “trump openly bribing people to vote for republicans. $5k per person if republicans hold the house and the senate?”

Stein was not alone in referencing bribery. Lisa Gilbert, co-president of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group, issued the following statement after Trump’s speech : “Trump knows he can’t do this, and yet he’s attempting to bribe voters with the false promise of cash to help his party win an election.”
But as a scholar of political and legal rhetoric , I think it’s worth further examining what the president said and whether his promise violated any law.

Paying voters to support a particular candidate, or promising government jobs in exchange for votes, has a long history in the United States. It was a staple of machine politics in big cities starting in the late 19th century.

The political scholar Simeon Nichter argues that it would be better to describe these practices as examples of “turnout buying.” He notes that “observers in various U.S. cities have complained that some politicians use ‘street money’ – small, unreported cash payments ostensibly used for legal get-out-the-vote efforts such as canvassing and transporting voters – as direct payments for turnout.”
What Nichter describes has made a comeback in our era.

Recall Elon Musk’s effort to ensure a Republican victory in a 2025 state Supreme Court election in Wisconsin. He spent millions in that effort and, as The Associated Press reported , offered “$1 million to people who voted in the Supreme Court election” to encourage them to vote.

In July 2026, the Wisconsin Elections Commission found enough evidence to refer citizen complaints about Musk’s behavior to a district attorney, “which can choose,” as the AP notes, “to bring criminal charges over violating the state law against election bribery.”
A month later, a state prosecutor said he could not prove Musk’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt and would not bring charges.
Because state and federal laws differ, we can’t extrapolate from the Wisconsin decision to Trump’s $5,000 promise.
Two provisions of federal law relating to vote buying were adopted by Congress and became law in 1948. Both treated that practice as a form of election interference.

The first reads as follows : “Whoever makes or offers to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote, or to vote for or against any candidate; and whoever solicits, accepts, or receives any such expenditure in consideration of his vote or the withholding of his vote; Shall be fined under this title or imprisoned … or both.”

The second prohibits offering government benefits “to any person as consideration, favor, or reward for any political activity or for the support of or opposition to any candidate or any political party in connection with any … election to any political office.”
Both provisions focus on the use of money or the promise of benefits to get individuals to vote in a particular way.

But Trump did not make his offer to any particular voter or set of voters. And, unlike Musk, he was acting as a public figure. The president’s promise was directed to all voters, not just to those who vote Republican.

John Day, a former federal prosecutor, compared Trump’s “dividend” to a pledge to deliver a tax break . “A promise to lower taxes also gives voters a financial reason to support a candidate, but that does not, by itself, make the promise a bribe,” Day told The New York Times.

In 1982, in Brown v. Hartlage, the Supreme Court weighed in on the legality of political figures promising financial benefits to voters. It found nothing wrong with the practice so long as the benefit was not offered as a quid pro quo to a particular voter.

Writing for a unanimous court, Justice William Brennan said that a political candidate “no less than any other person, has a First Amendment right to engage in the discussion of public issues and vigorously and tirelessly to advocate his own election and the election of other candidates.”

In his view, that right includes making statements about financial gains voters might receive if a candidate or a party wins an election, as long as they were “made openly and were subject to the criticism of his political opponent and to the scrutiny of the voters.” Such statements, Brennan added, were different from “corrupting private agreements and solicitations historically recognized as unprotected by the First Amendment.”
The Hartlage decision remains the applicable precedent today.

A year after the court’s decision, however, legal scholars Peter Aranson and Kenneth Shepsle argued that the Supreme Court decision countered several lower court decisions that had treated promises of the kind the high court approved “as analogous to bribes, which would turn the citizenry’s attention away from ‘proper’ public policy issues.”
Trump may view the question of whether Republicans retain control of Congress as just such an issue.

Whatever Trump’s view, commentators have observed that in Trump’s world, relationships are transactional. It is the deal that counts, not the values it promotes or undermines. So, the importance of Trump’s cash offer goes beyond the legal question of whether it is bribery, vote buying or a legitimate political promise.
It’s worth focusing attention on the virtues and vices of the transactional approach to politics, what it does to the character of U.S. political life and to the way Americans see the world.

One of Trump’s critics, the former presidential speechwriter Peter Wehner , describes what he calls “the great civic danger posed by Donald Trump” this way: “that the habits of his heart become the habits of our hearts: that his code of conduct becomes ours.”
Whether or not he is right, Wehner points Americans to a domain beyond law as the right place to assess the president’s promise of a “ Trump Dividend .”

articles.title: Here’s how teachers and parents can collaborate and help Michigan’s 1.4M students succeed
articles.author:
<name>Patricia Edwards, Professor of Education, Michigan State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/patricia-edwards-2735794"/>
paras: About 1.4 million Michigan students returned to the state’s K-12 public school classrooms this fall.
One of the most powerful influences on how these students will perform exists outside the classroom: the quality of the partnerships that schools and families establish with each other.

Establishing these partnerships may be easier than it sounds. Throughout more than four decades as an educator and researcher studying literacy and family engagement , I have learned that most families deeply care about their children’s education and want to work with teachers toward the best possible outcomes.

This message is especially timely in Michigan. Many students continue to experience challenges in reading following the COVID-19 pandemic. Only 39% of Michigan third graders scored proficient or advanced in English language arts on the M-STEP, an annual state exam, in the 2024-25 school year.

In 2024, Michigan students scored below the national average in reading on the National Assessment of Educational Progress . Michigan fourth graders averaged 209 , five points below the national average, while eighth graders averaged 255, compared with 257 nationally.

Although standardized test scores do not fully capture the breadth of students’ knowledge , abilities or potential, they can provide one useful indicator of how well students are developing literacy skills.

National studies also demonstrate that families want to play active roles in their children’s education. They show, too, that many parents seek clearer communication and more meaningful opportunities to collaborate with educators.

In my assessment, one of the most encouraging developments in family engagement research over the past two decades has been the growing recognition among researchers, educators and schools that parents are not simply volunteers who occasionally assist schools. They are co-educators whose knowledge, cultural wealth and lived experiences enrich children’s educational opportunities.
This understanding reflects a broader movement toward educational equity and shared responsibility for student success.

Families may be invited to attend conferences, literacy nights or workshops, but they are not always invited to share their knowledge or participate as equal partners in decisions about their children’s learning.

In my experience, families may feel that educators do not understand their cultural and linguistic practices. They may notice that communication flows primarily from school to home rather than in both directions, or that their knowledge of their own children is undervalued.

For families whose previous encounters with schools have involved judgment, exclusion or racism, or educators focusing on perceived shortcomings rather than recognizing families’ strengths, an invitation to participate does not automatically create understanding.

Some of my most formative lessons came during my early work with African American families in Louisiana. I began spending time with parents and listening carefully to what they understood schools were asking them to do at home.
Teachers frequently encouraged parents to “read to your child,” without explaining what meaningful reading might look like.

Some parents were uncertain about teachers’ expectations or viewed reading primarily as getting the words right. These experiences helped inspire Parents as Partners in Reading , a program I designed to help families support children’s literacy through interactive read-alouds that encourage conversation and making connections between books and children’s everyday lives.

In Louisiana, I showed rather than simply told them how they might make reading with their children more interactive and enjoyable. I modeled how to sit comfortably with a child, let the child hold the book and turn the pages, vary their voices, pause to ask questions, talk together about the pictures and follow the child’s interests and reactions.

Rather than prescribing a single “right” way to read together, these interactions gave parents opportunities to try different approaches, ask questions and discover what worked best for them and their children.

Parents then practiced these approaches with one another before using them. As their confidence increased, the interactions began to flow more naturally: Parents relied less on the strategies I had modeled and became more comfortable following their children’s lead, responding to their questions and comments and allowing conversations about the story to develop spontaneously.

I’ve watched educators transform their relationships with families once they begin viewing parents through their strengths rather than perceived flaws. Families know dimensions of their children that may never be visible during the school day: the child who loves to tell stories at the dinner table, or the child who is fascinated by cars or animals.

When educators listen to those stories, they gain information that can change how they understand and teach a child. Family engagement must also mean creating opportunities for educators to learn from families.

Instead of asking why families are not involved, they begin asking how schools can become more welcoming , more responsive and more collaborative. That shift in perspective often changes the entire culture of a school.
Here are a few ways educators can build relationships with families and vice versa:
Teachers shouldn’t wait until there is a problem to reach out to families. Relationships are strongest when schools communicate with families before challenges arise.
A welcoming phone call, a quick note celebrating something a child did well, an invitation to visit the classroom, or simply taking time to learn about a child’s interests can go a long way.

Parents can make a point of introducing themselves to their child’s teacher early in the school year. Parents might share something the teacher would find helpful to know about their child – what excites them, what they enjoy reading or doing at home, or what helps them feel confident as learners.
These early exchanges also communicate an important message: “I know my child in ways that can help you teach them, and I want us to work together.”
Families should hear from educators, but educators also need to hear from families. Communication is most meaningful when educators listen as much as they inform.

Educators can ask parents and caregivers: What are your hopes for your child this year? What should I know about your child that will help me be a better teacher? How does your child learn best? What is the easiest way for us to stay in touch?
Parents can ask teachers: “What are you noticing about my child as a reader and learner?” and “What are some things we can do at home that would reinforce what you are teaching at school?”

At some point, educators may need to talk with families about academic, behavioral or attendance concerns. Teachers can begin by sharing what the child does well and listening to what the family is seeing at home. Then invite their insights and perspectives: “Here is what I’m noticing. What are you seeing, and how can we work together?” This small shift – from presenting families with a problem to inviting them into a conversation – can transform a potentially difficult exchange into an opportunity for genuine partnership.

Families can listen carefully when teachers raise concerns and ask questions to better understand what the teacher is observing about their child. They can also share what they notice about their child at home, since children may demonstrate different strengths, behaviors and abilities in different settings.
Together, families and teachers can identify strategies to try at home and at school to address the concern and agree on a time to reconnect and discuss the child’s progress.

articles.title: CDC vs. Pennsylvania: Why conflicting public health messages jeopardize public safety
articles.author:
<name>Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/katrine-l-wallace-2626740"/>
paras: If you’ve been following the dispute between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., you probably know that it centers on the deaths of two infants in Lancaster County in late August 2026.

And you may be aware that despite the county coroner’s confirmation that one infant died due to measles, while the other’s death was “measles-associated,” the measles dashboard on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website counts neither death as of Sept. 10.

It’s easy to dismiss the squabble as political posturing between public officials. But as an epidemiologist who studies vaccine-preventable illnesses and health communication , I worry that for people seeking accurate information about how to keep their families safe – in this case, families in Lancaster County – there’s an enormous cost when health authorities no longer speak in one voice.
In the confusion that such rifts create, the public has no way of knowing which disagreements are about evidence and which are driven by ideology and narrative control.

The U.S. government issues a certificate for every death, confirming its underlying cause following a physician’s examination. The death certificate poses a narrow question: What single condition set in motion the chain of events that ended in this person’s death? This is recorded as the cause of death.

Because measles is what the CDC calls a notifiable condition, or a reportable disease , measles deaths get added to a national count. Contributing conditions go on a separate line in the document and are not counted.

Nobody disputes that both infants had measles when they died. The argument is which line on the death certificate “measles” belongs on. The Pennsylvania Department of Health has called both deaths measles-associated . This term is used when there’s evidence the person had measles, but there’s no settled official cause of death yet. It’s a holding category, not a verdict.

The job of determining the official cause – that is, certifying a death – falls to the county coroner. Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni concluded that for one of the infants, a newborn boy who died in mid-August, the cause was a ruptured spleen unrelated to the measles infection. For a 6-week-old girl who died Aug. 18, he found that measles was the cause .

These are not competing conclusions. They come from two different systems asking two different questions. County coroners’ decisions on cause of death are legal finding, made one case at a time, that feed national vital statistics .

State health departments, on the other hand, run disease surveillance. They track who got sick and who died during an outbreak so they can contain it. Surveillance moves in days because it has to; death certification moves in weeks because it should. The two rarely line up in real time.
While the apparent divergence between county and state data was basically a technicality, the exchange between Shapiro and Kennedy was more of a brawl.

Shapiro announced the infants’ deaths on Aug. 25 and blamed anti-vaccine rhetoric for falling vaccination rates and increasing cases. The CDC posted condolences on the social media platform X , using Pennsylvania’s language calling the deaths measles-associated.

But in response, Kennedy suggested the deaths might have been fabricated by a member of the governor’s staff. Two days after Shapiro’s announcement, the CDC walked back its post , expressing appreciation for Kennedy’s efforts to clarify conflicting information from Pennsylvania officials about whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles.

Then, in an unusual move, on Aug. 30 , the CDC changed the death count on its measles dashboard from 2 to an asterisk, with a footnote stating that the National Center for Health Statistics currently has no death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause.
No new evidence arrived in those two days that would explain the CDC’s new position.

HHS now says it is working with a national network of disease tracking experts on a standardized case definition for measles deaths. Standard case definitions exist for measles infections but not for measles deaths, for the simple reason that until recently, dying from measles in the U.S. was an extremely rare occurrence: Between 2001 and 2022 , the U.S. recorded roughly 4,000 cases and three deaths.

But writing a definition in the middle of a count – and applying it to a single state’s deaths – is a departure from protocol. Previously, during outbreaks in Texas and New Mexico in 2025, the CDC did count three measles-associated deaths while they were still being investigated. Declining to do so now is inconsistent and confusing , and breeds mistrust.

Unnamed officials told news outlets that CDC Director Erica Schwartz removed the deaths at Kennedy’s request , after CDC staff had accepted the state’s data. HHS disputes this, and Kennedy said in a post on X that the coroner’s finding – that the newborn boy’s death was caused by a ruptured spleen – vindicated federal caution .

A parent sifting through all this information has no way to gauge who is right. The usual shortcut – check the CDC numbers on the measles dashboard – now yields an asterisk leading to a footnote that contradicts statements from state officials, a county coroner and the agency’s own condolence post from 10 days earlier. There’s no neutral tiebreaker left, which means the decision falls back on which institution you already trusted most.
While that argument played out, a second rift was widening on a different track.

On Sept. 2, four physician groups – the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America – issued their own vaccine recommendations for the fall respiratory season.

The pediatricians association had already split from the CDC’s childhood immunization schedule in 2025 , ending a 30-year practice of publishing one agreed-upon set of recommendations for families. What’s new is that three more societies have now joined this public health separatist movement, and that the split has extended to the shots most adults get.

On influenza, the physician groups’ advice matches the CDC’s: Everyone 6 months and older should get a flu vaccine. On COVID-19 they go further, recommending vaccination for children 6 to 23 months, whereas the CDC tells parents to consult a doctor.

For decades, the CDC has issued fall vaccine recommendations each year, offering a unified slate of federal advice for everyone across the U.S. to follow. Now, with the federal advisory committee that makes those recommendations sidelined and embroiled in a legal battle , the agency has issued no new federal vaccine guidance for this season. The four physician groups stepped forward to fill the gap.
Yet technically, the CDC’s previous seasonal recommendations – and its revised childhood immunization schedule – still stand, creating a confusing doubling of critical health guidance.

Measles is among the most contagious diseases known. Roughly 1 to 3 in 1,000 children who catch it die, and in 2025, 11% of cases required a hospital stay. A 2025 study put the average cost at roughly US$43,000 per case .

The national case count reached 3,134 on Sept. 4, the highest since 1991. As of the same date, Pennsylvania had recorded 624 cases – 91 in the previous week. More than 40% of Pennsylvania’s cases have been in Lancaster County.
Parents must now reconcile a recently revised federal immunization schedule, a set of physician-society recommendations that departs from it, a state count of two deaths and a national count of none.

Each of those positions has an institution behind it. None of them explains how it relates to the others – and that is what’s most damaging. Public trust doesn’t only collapse when officials lie. It erodes when people are handed different information that can’t be squared, or misleading information, and are left to sort it out alone.

articles.title: ‘The Uprising’ shows how medieval people weren’t so obedient after all
articles.author:
<name>Joëlle Rollo-Koster, Professor Emerita of Medieval History, University of Rhode Island</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/joelle-rollo-koster-1286920"/>
paras: For decades, I’ve been showing my medieval history students the “ autonomous collective ” scene from the 1975 film “ Monty Python and the Holy Grail .”

The clip is funny because it features two medieval peasants haranguing King Arthur while using the lexicon of a modern political Marxist. When Arthur explains that he was their king because the Lady of the Lake gave him Excalibur, one of the peasants objects: “Supreme executive power derives from a mandate from the masses, not from some farcical aquatic ceremony!”
It also subverts the assumption that medieval people were politically passive, with resistance to abuses of authority largely absent before the Renaissance and the Protestant Reformation.
But far from being an age of unquestioning obedience, the Middle Ages – the period from roughly 500 to 1500 – witnessed a remarkable number of popular revolts and collective political action.

Even if they didn’t speak in the language of Karl Marx, ordinary people back then held strong views about the working of political authority . And when they believed authorities had violated their obligations or lost their legitimacy, they routinely challenged rulers, bishops, tax collectors and urban elites.
In the 11th and 12th centuries, northern French peasants famously resisted carrying out the work or paying the money that they owed to the lords who controlled the land they farmed.
But perhaps the most well-known insurrection is the English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 , the subject of the new film “ The Uprising ,” starring Andrew Garfield.

After the first wave of the Black Death in 1348 created a massive labor shortage in Europe, workers were better positioned to negotiate for higher wages and better conditions. Serfs – peasants bound to the land and subject to a lord’s authority – increasingly pushed back against oppressive feudal obligations.

But kings and lords resisted change. In 1351, England’s King Edward III decreed the Statute of Laborers , which froze wages, derailing any aspiration for social mobility among the peasant class. Resentment continued to build with recurring episodes of the plague.

Then, in 1381, Edward’s grandson and successor – 12-year-old King Richard II – instituted a one-time tax of 12 pence to raise funds for England’s ongoing war with France. Because the tax was charged per person rather than according to wealth, it placed a particularly heavy burden on poorer families.

The people had had enough: Crowds attacked tax collectors and eventually organized into a larger movement, burning houses, castles and the records that documented their obligations to their lords. They killed government officials before marching to London to confront the king.
The king met the rebels and pledged to abolish the poll tax and serfdom, while lowering the rent of agricultural land.
He later recanted those promises: His forces hunted down the rebels, quashing the uprising.

Insurrections like the English Peasants’ Revolt erupted, in part, because in cities across Europe, regular people had cultivated a strong tradition of collective action. There was broad membership in guilds , which were voluntary associations of merchants and craftsmen. Then there were neighborhood religious confraternities , which were akin to today’s religious mutual-aid societies. Together, they gave ordinary townspeople networks through which they could organize around shared interests and grievances.

Over in France, the Hundred Years’ War caused a breakdown in authority. People were increasingly being asked to pay taxes they couldn’t afford. Unpaid troops routinely raided the countryside, and the French military suffered a number of significant military defeats.

In 1358, the Jacques – a derogatory name for members of the lower French peasantry – razed noble estates and killed members of the aristocracy. They also joined forces with the Parisian bourgeoisie and the city’s chief political leader, Étienne Marcel, to fight for a greater voice in French government.

The rage underpinning the violence of what became known as the Jacquerie emerged from the fact that the same aristocracy that demanded so much of them could not fulfill their basic part of the bargain: protect them.

A little over a decade later, violence erupted in Florence, Italy. The city-state was an industrial juggernaut ruled by guilds, but their representatives all belonged to the urban elite. The lower classes of the textile industry weren’t represented by guilds and were largely disenfranchised. So the Ciompi – low-level woolworkers – demanded a role in the guild system. Those demands fell on deaf ears.

In June 1378, the Ciompi revolted and attacked government offices. Thanks to their efforts, they won participation in the guild system for four years, up until the city’s old powerful merchant elite dissolved their lower guilds.
Nor was the other main source of authority, the church, immune to attack.
When power vacuums emerged after the death of an abbot, bishop or even the pope, regular people routinely ransacked their property, taking with them a substantial amount of the dead’s movables.

“From various reports we are aware of the perverse and wholly detestable practice of certain people, who at the death of the bishop break in like enemies and rob his house, like thieves make off with his belongings, set fire to the homes on his estate, and with fierce and savage barbarity cut down his grape vines and orchards.”

Early Christian elections were initially open to entire congregations. Though these elections often gave the lion’s share of voting power to the wealthy and well-connected, there was the general understanding that everyone would play a role: “ vox populi, vox Dei ,” or “the voice of the people is the voice of God.”

However, by the end of the 13th century, the papacy had successfully established its authority over both ordinary people and secular rulers. On religious matters, there would no longer be public input. Instead, beginning in 1274, a conclave of cardinals elected the pope. The pope, sometimes still under the influence of higher lords, then nominated abbots and bishops.
The voice of the people had largely vanished. Nevertheless, they made themselves heard.
An April 1314 papal election in Carpentras, a small city in southeastern France, turned so violent that it delayed the naming of a new pope for nearly two years.

Deadlocked over the candidates, the cardinals dragged out the election for so long that frustrated locals attacked the episcopal palace where the conclave was being held. Cardinals and their staff fled and delayed until August 1316, when, under the protection of the French king’s forces, they nominated Pope John XXII .

Over 60 years later, in March 1378, Pope Gregory XI died. Amid threats from a crowd demanding an Italian pope, the cardinals elected Urban VI , an Italian, the following month. But over the ensuing months, the cardinals soured on Urban and declared their election invalid on the grounds that they had acted under duress. They elected a rival pope, triggering the Great Western Schism , during which two competing papal courts existed from 1378 to 1417.
Violence could also erupt for seemingly minor affronts.

In October 1367, Pope Urban V was in Viterbo, Italy. The pope and his court were French. The Viterbese took offense when papal court officials washed a little dog in their fountain of Piano di Scarano, which served as a source of drinking water. A confrontation followed, which escalated into a two-day uprising . The fountain was destroyed, and the pope and his cardinals were forced to take refuge in the Rocca Albornoz, the papal fortress.
Ideologies have evolved and technologies have advanced, but the fundamental struggle over who wields power, how authority earns legitimacy, and how compliance is enforced remains strikingly familiar.
The levers that leaders pull – taxation, welfare, infrastructure projects, propaganda, law enforcement – are largely the same, too.

Yet medieval folks understood that authority was a two-way street. When those in power didn’t hold up their end of the bargain, they were quick to resist, demand accountability and challenge authority.
In this sparring over power and consent, we can see, as one of Monty Python’s peasants put it, “the violence inherent in the system.”

articles.title: Why the Trump administration’s bid to end diversity efforts at nonprofit schools is likely to get tied up in court
articles.author:
<name>Elizabeth Schmidt, Professor of Practice in Public Policy, Nonprofit Organizations, and Social & Environmental Enterprises, UMass Amherst</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/elizabeth-schmidt-338437"/>
paras: The Trump administration wants to strip all nonprofit colleges, universities and private K-12 schools of their tax-exempt status if any of their programs designed to help students uses race as a criterion for eligibility.

This change is included in a rule the Treasury Department and Internal Revenue Service proposed on Sept. 3, 2026 . The rule could take effect after May 31, 2027, following a two-month-long comment period – as long as it’s not blocked or delayed by the legal challenges likely to arise.

As a nonprofit law scholar who helps nonprofit leaders understand the legal issues they face , I believe this latest salvo in the Trump administration’s attempt to end racial preferences stretches U.S. law so far that it will likely be tied up in court for years.

The proposed rule states that private schools aren’t eligible for tax-exempt status if they have any school-administered or -supported program that “discriminates on the basis of race, color, or national or ethnic origin … for any purpose.”

The regulations do not define the word “discriminate” in this context, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has made clear that the Trump administration considers programs that have diversity goals to be a form of discrimination.

Private K-12 schools, colleges, universities and professional and trade schools would be subject to this rule, including all academic and athletic programs as well as all scholarships and admissions policies having anything to do with efforts to increase diversity.

The proposed rule would not apply to religious schools that make admitting people who adhere to the school’s religion a priority. Nor would it apply to public universities, but I believe the language is broad enough to apply to the foundations that provide scholarships to students at public universities.
At this point, many key details about the rule remain unclear.
The IRS estimates that this rule would affect 18,000 private schools attended by 750,000 students at all levels of instruction.

All private schools that are nonprofits depend on this tax exemption, both to save money on income and property tax bills and to attract donations . Without these benefits in place, tuition bills at nonprofit schools could skyrocket and the financial pressures many colleges and universities already face would increase.

Americans gave about US$92 billion in charitable donations to private schools in 2025, which mostly supported higher education. That funding covers an average of about 10% of college and university budgets .

A change in the rules could also complicate schools’ relationships with their donors, alter the distribution of scholarships and lead to significant legal bills, as the government itself has acknowledged .

The proposed rule hinges on the Trump administration’s definition of racial discrimination: that any kind of racial preference is wrong and grounds for terminating government support – even when it’s meant to address past injustices, like the decades of systemic discrimination that followed the end of slavery in the United States.
The IRS’ explanation of this rule alludes to many legal precedents, including two significant U.S. Supreme Court decisions.

With its Bob Jones University v. United States ruling, the court found in 1983 that a university banning interracial dating and marriage provided the IRS with the legal grounds to revoke its tax-exempt status .

And the court found in 2023, in its Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard ruling, that colleges and universities that accept government funding cannot consider race in their admissions policies without violating the equal protection clause of the Constitution.
There is evidence that the government lacks the authority to implement this proposed rule.

Educational groups, such as EdTrust and the American Association of University Professors , have expressed their opposition to the proposed changes. Legal scholars, such as Philip Hackney, Ellen Aprill, Daryll Jones and Brian Galle , have explained why the rule is likely illegal.

Two courts found on June 30, 2026, that the Department of Education did not have the authority to alter student loan forgiveness rules for the employees of nonprofits . I expect to see opponents of the proposed rule to use those cases to support this argument.
Even if the courts determine the IRS does have authority to issue this rule, they will have the final say as to whether the agency has interpreted congressional intent correctly.
Legal scholars are also saying that the Trump administration’s interpretation of prior Supreme Court cases regarding discrimination at schools with tax-exempt status is incorrect.

They point out that the Harvard admissions case was limited to colleges and universities that accepted public funding, and it provided some narrow exceptions. The proposed regulation would apply to all private schools, without exception, even if they don’t receive federal funding.

Further, the Bob Jones ruling stressed that a nonprofit’s tax-exempt status could only be revoked on “fundamental public policy” grounds when the activity in question so shocked the community conscience that it undermined any other benefit the institution conferred. It based its opinion on 30 years of evidence from all three branches of government to show that this kind of prejudice violated fundamental public policy.

The Trump administration may be unable to show that the public’s perspective regarding diversity, equity and inclusion has changed that much. It faces numerous lawsuits challenging its definition of racial discrimination, and the American public remains overwhelmingly in favor of diversity, equity and inclusion policies.

Law professor Roger Colinvaux has also pointed out that interpreting the term “discrimination” to mean that organizations can no longer remedy past discrimination runs counter to the legal definition of the term “charitable,” which means to help those in need. Treasury Department regulations define charitable activities as helping “the poor and disadvantaged” and eliminating “prejudice and discrimination.”

Finally, as Alexander Reid, a prominent attorney who specializes in tax exemptions, noted in a letter to the IRS , the proposed rule raises significant First Amendment issues of freedom of speech , religion, association and institutional autonomy. That’s because it would affect choices that all private schools make that are essential to their identities and expression of ideas.

Two years ago, the federal government supported a definition of racial discrimination that is vastly different from the definition the Trump administration now holds, and a new administration could come up with still another meaning. The lawsuits that will surely challenge this proposed rule will help to determine the legal meaning of racial discrimination – and Congress could weigh in as well.
In the meantime, many nonprofit schools may end their programs that are designed to address the results of past discrimination out of a fear of potentially losing their tax-exempt status.
I would not be surprised to see other kinds of nonprofits taking similar precautions as well, on the assumption that the Trump administration will apply this logic more broadly in the future.
The IRS will need to respond to the major themes addressed in the comments it receives by Nov. 3, 2026. It may change the rule before it issues a final version.
And even if the rule were to be finalized on schedule, I would expect extensive litigation could delay or prevent its implementation.
Elizabeth Schmidt is a Senior Research Fellow at UMass Amherst. She is also President of Rules of the Road for Nonprofits, LLC.

articles.title: Feds Hope to Boost Homebuilding with 'ROAD to Housing' Act
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: In July, the U.S. Congress quietly passed a significant update to federal housing policy that builders and housing advocates are saying could provide a major boost to production. The bill took effect without President Trump's signature, a policy that was initially introduced in 2025 as the Renewing Opportunity in the American Dream (ROAD) to Housing Act.

The National Low Income Housing Coalition (NLIHC) hailed the bill as "first major bipartisan housing package to become law since the 1990s." Shaun Donovan, CEO of the housing finance nonprofit Enterprise , called the bill "the most significant piece of housing legislation" in decades.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

But advocates have also warned the bill's impact ultimately rests on implementation steps that federal government will need to take, with Congress backing up the smorgasbord of regulatory changes with direct funding to really unlock their potential.

The bill does not allocate new dollars or directly change low income housing tax credits (LIHTC) – the primary way that the federal government funnels money to affordable housing developers in a post-Reagan America. Housing advocates have pledged a push to secure funding to the unfunded program in the year ahead, but that could prove challenging given competing priorities and budget deficits.

LIHTC counts on banks and other financial institutions applying for tax credits to lower their federal tax bills, while also meeting regulatory obligations to invest in their local communities – a bit of a sweetheart deal for the banks. When the federal government lowers the corporate tax rate – like it did under Trump 1.0 in 2017 – that in turn depresses interest in LIHTC , leading to less funding being available to affordable housing developers.

On one hand, Trump's second term has surprisingly coincided with the largest overhaul of federal housing policy in decades – after he unsuccessfully attempted to hold the bill hostage to a voter ID measure he was pushing. On the other hand, Trump's staffing cuts imperil implementation of the reforms. Plus, Trump tax cuts passed in his first term continue to depress investor interest in LIHTC, and efforts in Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" to juice LIHTC demand with lower bonding thresholds (while lowering taxes on wealthiest Americans) can only bear so much fruit in a low-tax environment, especially when plenty of other headwinds are impeding nonprofit builders.

Even without funding or broader reforms to LIHTC (such as a higher corporate tax rate to drive up interest in tax credits), the ROAD to Housing Act includes plenty of provisions that could have a significant impact either way. In all, the act is more than 400 pages long and features 59 provisions.

Mike Kingsella CEO of Up For Growth , a national coalition pushing for housing abundance, noted housing supply provisions were embedded in the act during a recent housing panel hosted by the Housing Development Consortium of King County (HDC), which I attended as moderator. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) could play a larger role in encouraging zoning reforms.

"Section 107 housing supply frameworks was initially led by a very interesting duo of members of Congress, Mike Flood, a Republican conservative from Nebraska, and Brittany Pettersen, a Dem member from Colorado," Kingsella said. "Essentially, what this provision will do, is stand up a federal task force on best practice land use and zoning policies. HUD will aggregate those best practices and establish federal model codes, both for state legislatures to take up vis-a-vis similar actions to what Olympia has taken up recently, around, for example, eliminating exclusionary zoning, it will also generate model local zoning codes that cities and towns around the country can pick up."

The Middle Housing Law passed in 2023 was Washington State's nudge to end exclusionary zonin g within cities, and it was followed up with statewide parking reform that limited cities ability to heap onerous parking mandates on builders. The federal version of this phase out to exclusionary zoning ended up more as a suggestion than having any major teeth behind it, but it's still momentum toward righting a historic wrong, Kingsella argued.

"Now, this isn't without precedent," Kingsella said. "It was, in fact, the federal government, the Standard Zoning Enabling Act, that was the Johnny Appleseed of exclusionary zoning around the country, and so this is an opportunity for Congress and the federal government to correct a wrong that that occurred not over just a few months over 100 years ago. So that's a provision we're quite excited about."

One way the federal government intends to nudge local governments toward pro-growth policies and zoning reform is through new stipulations rewarding pro-growth jurisdictions with larger awards via the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) program, which distributes about $3.3 billion in federal funds annually.

"What this provision does is it establishes a scrutiny pool of CDBG recipients, and within that recipient pool, HUD will assess – and this will be based on a clear and objective formula established in statute – are you meeting your fair share of housing production?" Kingsella said. "In other words, and it's a very simple structure: Are you above or below the median point line out of jurisdictions in that scrutiny pool? If you're falling below the average jurisdiction in a scrutiny pool, you stand to lose up to 10% of your formulaic CDBG each year. The flip is that if you exceed the 50% median mark, you're going to get bonused out extra CDBG dollars based on the number of units that your community has produced."
If it's able to trigger this bonus, Seattle would have help in expanding its lead in producing the most new affordable housing units of any metropolitan area across the country over the last decade.

Another provision will make it easier for homebuilders to avoid going through the time-consuming National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process, with the federal government recognizing that process is often duplicative of state and local regulatory processes and laws.

Yet another provision could boost modular housing construction by overhauling HUD's Manufactured Housing Building Code, removing the costly requirement that manufactured homes have a steel chassis. "It's arguable that this could be the most impactful provision out of the entire bill," Kingsella said.

"You have to have a steel chassis, and that's a relic of history, right? Back in the 1960s and 70s, when we were building manufactured housing, practically speaking, you have to take them down the road and to install on a pad and deliver to the user," Kingsella said. "Today, we're in a world where you have offsite construction, you have construction happening in factories... and you have panels built, and these things are getting assembled, but not built on site. Even though, in terms of the envelope and the product type, we're talking about effectively the same thing. It does not qualify as manufactured housing per the old 1960s HUD code. So you can think of this as really modernizing the code in a way that we're creating a new national building code for anything factory built that has huge implications for the scaling of modular and offsite construction, which is something that I know leadership in Washington State is quite focused on."

Beyond the need for funding, another obstacle to implementing the act's housing reform is staff capacity at HUD. The department has seen an exodus since Trump took office for the second time, in large part due to cuts to positions via the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

"We're looking at a HUD that has had upwards of 30% staff [reduction in force] due to DOGE actions and decision making in this administration," Kingsella said. "I am concerned. I think many of my colleagues in DC are concerned with the capacity of HUD to effectively implement many of these provisions. So we are playing the long game."

Architect and planner Jess Zimbabwe, who is executive director of the firm Environmental Works and also was a panelist at the HDC event last month, noted that reduced capacity will be acutely felt for the provision instructing HUD to create pre-approved housing plans as a nudge to reduce zoning hurdles.

"This question about pre-approved housing plans...that sounds like a great idea in a different version of HUD, where you know Public Policy Development and Research, the the division of HUD that will eventually probably pull those pre-approved plans together is at like 75% or 80% reduced force because of DOGE cuts from last year," Zimbabwe said. "So nobody's pulling that together right now. But it's a framework in place that when there is when that is funded and staffed, it could be hugely impactful."
She added that Washington state stands to benefit since it's already innovating in this space and should be positioned to trigger incentives, like the CDBG boost.

While the ROAD to Housing Act passed with huge margins in each chamber, the issue of funding could be more contentious and push lawmakers more firmly to their ideological camps. Without those funding strings attached, the bill passed in the Senate on June 21 with a vote of 85-5, and in the House on June 22 with a vote of 358-32.

The other challenge is overcoming negative trends in the business cycle and in LIHTC demand from banks and financial institutions. Panelists who work in LIHTC shared pessimism it would be fixed overnight. Elizabeth Murphy, who is a manager on Baker Tilly’s Development Advisory Services team, did not predict big changes in LIHTC investor appetite.

"It's great that they increase the public welfare investment cap," Murphy said. "It obviously makes it a lot easier. And it's great – not part of this legislation – but we also had the reduction of the 50% test, and in the bond program, we have you know a higher cap on 9% credits. Those are all excellent policy changes, but until the market meets demand, I don't see like pricing changing all that much or investor appetite changing all that much."

Jackie Moynihan, senior policy advisor at Washington State Housing Finance Commission, agreed with Murphy, noting investors ultimately drive the LIHTC market. That adds uncertainty, but also opportunity if the feds somehow thread the needle.

"All these other pieces around gap financing are huge, and so, if also appropriations comes through, and the flexibility in different programs and the streamlining... Like if all of these pieces came together, that would be super impactful," Moynihan said. "I think we definitely operate in this sphere of not any one thing does get it done. We need all the things to move and get done."
In her introduction, HDC Executive Director Patience Malaba agreed the aspirations of the bill hinged on implementation.

"We have the first legislation in 40 years, massive legislation on housing at the federal level coming out of Congress," Malaba said. "That on its own is a critical milestone to celebrate and elevate. And then there's so much more for us to do on what gets implemented and how do we make that happen."
HDC pledged to mobilize its community to keep advocating and pushing for funding to bring to life some unfunded elements on the plan.

"How do we track what needs to move through appropriations and activate folks on the ground to push for those appropriations, whether that's fiscal year 27 or other cycles where investments will be needed to operationalize some of the great ideas around supporting housing supply, innovation and construction methods, and so much more that's been included in the legislation," Malaba said.
Congress has passed its biggest housing reform in decades, and yet so much work remains.

articles.title: El Pastorcito Taqueria brought the tacos — It’s also working on a fresh tortilla machine and even more Mexico vibes on Broadway
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: El Pastorcito Taqueria recently opened on Capitol Hill, with more big plans already underway—from importing a custom tortilla machine straight from Mexico to an upcoming dining room remodel.
“People like the food, they keep coming,” owner Fabian Munoz said.

A tortilla machine is on order from Mexico, though it will take time to arrive. “That will take two or three months because they are making the machine, then we have to import it,” Munoz said. “It takes time and money.” The masa and meat will still be made in-house, and the machine takes over the part of the job that is nearly impossible to keep up with by hand.

El Pastorcito Taqueria opened at 314 Broadway E in the former Broadway Grill space this summer. Co-owned by Pedro Barragan Bautista , who also operates the original location in Kent along with Mr. Cammaron Bar & Grill and the El Pollo Rey food truck, the taqueria brings the flavors of Tijuana to Capitol Hill with trompo tacos and tortas .
The Mexico vibe is part of the pitch. Munoz pointed to the Coca-Cola tables and chairs, the promotional furniture restaurants get free from beverage distributors in Mexico.

“If you step into a Mexican restaurant, they have all the promo tables because it’s free there,” he said. “That’s how they do business there.” He called it a landmark back home, and it’s the feeling he’s going for on the Hill. “We want people to feel like they are in Mexico.”
El Pastorcito is now part of what has become a rich taco community along Broadway.

In March , brother chefs Rey and Osiel Gastelum opened Tacos Cometa on the Pike/Pine end of the street after growing a devoted following over the previous year on the edge of Cal Anderson Park as part of the neighborhood’s wild — and delicious — nightlife street food scene.
In 2025 , Carmelo’s Tacos expanded on Broadway as it has grown from its start in a counter space inside the Hillcrest Market .
Other Mexican joints include Broadway veteran La Cocina which has been serving the neighborhood for more than 45 years.
Asked what sets his taqueria apart from others on Capitol Hill, Munoz didn’t overthink it. “We have the pastor tacos,” he said. “And our vibe.”

He has also been adjusting things behind the scenes. After fielding complaints about the carne asada, he asked his meat distributor for something better than the standard grade they had used. “He gave us another option,” Munoz said.

A remodel is planned, too. “We’re going to start working on the back,” he said. “We’re going to paint the walls and put up TVs.” The plan is for the dining room and front area to feel like the same restaurant wherever you sit.

For now, Munoz’s pitch to the neighborhood is simple. “I would like to invite people to come try the restaurant,” he said. “We want to keep working on the quality. We want to keep working on the space.”
El Pastorcito Taqueria is located at 314 Broadway E. Follow @elpastorcitotaqueria for updates.

articles.title: Seattle Group Finalizing Deal to Reopen the Egyptian Theater
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Twenty-three years ago, I found myself next to a hospital bed. My mother was on it and on life support. The doctor entered the room and painted a bleak picture; and I said to him: I know, I know, it’s serious. After hours of sitting by the bed, watching my mother and the machine that kept her alive, a nurse recommended that I take a break and give my mind a little distraction. I decided to watch a movie. I left the hospital, walked down to the Egyptian Theater, bought a ticket, took a seat, and the movie, Alejandro González Iñárritu’s 21 Grams , opened with Sean Penn in a hospital room and on life support. I did not know whether to laugh or cry. Wherever you are, death is always there.

I bring this little story up because it expresses how closely my life is tied to the Egyptian, which temporarily closed its doors in 2024 after a pipe broke and flooded the theater. It then permanently closed in 2025 when SIFF decided not to renew its 10-year lease of the space. Though a few events have occurred at the Egyptian since its closure, it’s been mostly dead: closed doors, dark windows, empty displays for movie posters. But that might change in the near future.

A group called WFLM Seattle is in the process of closing a deal with Seattle College, the owners of the Egyptian Theater, that would bring it back to life, back to reality. A member of this group, Ben Redder, says they are on the verge of finalizing the lease. (Seattle College informed me that it will make the deal public as soon as it is signed by both parties.)

“We’ve been in talks with Seattle College since mid-February,” says Redder over the phone. “We started WFLM for the purpose of taking over the Egyptian. We made a plan. Got supporters. But we’ve already screened a documentary there about Lenny Wilkins , three-time NBA Hall of Famer, at the theater. It was a big success. His family was in attendance. There were several NBA Hall of Famers there, too. This happened in August, and it sold out. So it was only natural to take the next big step. Get a lease and program shows.”

When the deal is done, WFLM, which includes Elias Savage, Scotty Wright, and Lanna Hed, plans to model the new Egyptian’s programming along the lines of Santa Ana’s Frida Cinema , which basically screens the best of the best and the best of the worst films. WFLM will not, like Tasveer Film Center, which replaced Columbia City’s Ark Lodge Cinema earlier this year, show first-run movies, but stick to repertory flicks, crowd pleasers, and forgotten gems. WFLM also wants to bring back midnight movies, which were once a key component of Capitol Hill nightlife.

“The theater is nearly in immaculate shape,” says Redder, who was assistant manager at the Cinerama until 2020 (when it closed due to Covid). After working at Scarecrow Video for two years, he became the general manager of Cinerama when SIFF took over the theater in 2023, but he was laid off in June 2025. “[The Egyptian] just needs some touch-ups here and there. Maybe some paint on a few walls. So, we’ll need a little time to make some improvements, make sure the equipment is working. If all goes well, we hope to be up and running by the end of the year.” And so it is. Life does sometimes conquer death.

The race kicked off at Denny Way & Dexter Ave at 5:41pm as bus 8266 crossed Dexter Ave.
The bus immediately left almost everyone in the dust. After the first block, only a few runners kept up with the bus.

The bus picked up dozens of riders at the stops near Westlake Ave and Fairview Ave before barrelling towards the finish line, behind just three runners. Bus 8266 finished at 5:45pm, clocking in a total race time of 4 minutes for the half-mile race. Last year, the bus took 21 minutes.

articles.title: Metro Prevails in 'Race the L8' Rematch Thanks to New Bus Lanes
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: It was never going to be a fair race. Not with the new secret weapon in Metro's arsenal, a bright stretch of red paint extending all the way from Tilikum Place in Belltown to I-5. It's a bus lane that previous Seattle leaders had thought unthinkable, but at 5pm Tuesday more than 150 transit advocates showed up in South Lake Union to race a Route 8 bus up Denny Way, and got smoked by King County Metro.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Well, most of them got smoked. Three runners, all of whom had clearly been getting their training days in, did manage to beat the 8 to Denny Way and Stewart Street by a few seconds, thanks in large part to extra bus dwell time to handle a sizable crowd of riders at Westlake Avenue.
Most of Tuesday's "racers" proceeded much more slowly than that first 8 coach did. Many even got to wave as another bus passed by on the way up the hill.

The event was a rematch, after last July's "Race the L8" saw cha-cha dancers, leapfroggers, and even someone driving a tiny car on the sidewalk ultimately beat a Route 8 coach up Denny Way. A whimsical illustration of the prior state of the infamous L8 bus, the event attracted significant media attention and shined a light on the issue in a brand new way.

The topic of the slow 8 was catapulted into the Seattle mayor's race, with then-candidate Katie Wilson (a regular Route 8 rider) making the trek up the hill with everyone else. The issue formed a clear contrast with former Mayor Bruce Harrell, whose administration was closed off to the idea of expanding bus lanes on Denny Way and reversed plans to add Third Avenue bus lanes in Belltown.

That attention turned into Mayor Wilson's very first executive order after taking office in January, spelling out a compact timeline to get red paint on the ground – this year. The road redesign included a reroute for traffic headed to I-5 onramps, which previously turned Denny Way into essentially a parking lot.

Things are very different 14 months later. With the new bus lane, Route 8 buses are traveling three times faster during the afternoon and evening peak period, according to preliminary data relayed by Wilson herself Tuesday. Riders traveling between Dexter Avenue and Fairview Avenue saved an average of 3.5 minutes – a huge amount multiplied across all of the route's riders – with the Route 8 recording its fastest travel times on Denny Way in at least seven years.

Racers saw even more dramatic bus acceleration in action Tuesday amid rush hour traffic. The bus took 21 minutes to complete the traffic-clogged half-mile race course back in 2025. On Tuesday, the bus took just four minutes – a staggering five times faster than the last race.

The reliability of the route has dramatically improved as well. Metro's trip times along the corridor varied by less than one minute last week, when it would oftentimes be more than 10 minutes without the bus lanes.

"Last summer, I joined many of you here to race the L8, and we saw firsthand what Route 8 riders have experienced for years and years and years: busses full of people stuck in traffic on one of the busiest corridors in our city," Wilson said in remarks to the crowd. "Riders and community advocates have been pushing for better Route 8 service for years, and I was proud to stand with them then. And I am very proud that we are here today celebrating real progress."

Making this project happen didn't just require a shift in mayoral priorities, it required a shift in departmental mindset. Last year, the assessment of a multi-block bus lane on eastbound Denny Way from inside the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) was that the street grid couldn't handle such constriction of general-purpose traffic.

"This traffic congestion is expected to impact the ability of buses to access the bus lane and could result in backups in the bus lane itself," an SDOT blog post from last August stated. "Overall traffic would likely be significantly worse along Denny Way, with estimates showing general purpose travel times nearly doubling during peak travel times."
That traffic nightmare never came to pass.

"We were told that it was not possible to put a bus lane on Denny Way," Nick Sattele, who co-founded the Fix the L8 campaign in 2023, told racers Tuesday. "That the delay for drivers would be too high. It would destroy the bus, the transportation network. It would blow up traffic in South Lake Union. But we knew they were wrong because their studies didn't incorporate that drivers would take different routes, or that some drivers maybe would become transit riders as well."

Just a few weeks after the bus lanes were installed in mid-August, the traffic grid seems to be adapting to the new normal on Denny Way just fine. Travel times to Capitol Hill or I-5 by car are not dramatically up, and stretches of the road often look deserted during rush hour compared to past years. The traffic model was wrong, a fact that should have broad implications for transportation planning in Seattle way beyond the confines of Denny Way.

In addition to a faster bus, the project also resulted in safer sidewalks with fewer conflict points with car traffic. The former Yale Avenue intersection that used to clog the sidewalk and road with I-5 traffic has been curbed off to car traffic and is now a small pedestrian plaza where advocates congregated and mingled after the race.

Another remarkable aspect of the Denny Way project is the speed with which it was implemented. Bus lanes have traditionally taken years to be implemented in Seattle, subjected to substantial planning timelines or tied to larger capital projects. A northbound bus lane for the city's second-busiest bus, the Route 7 on Rainier Avenue, entered planning in 2022 and wasn't actually implemented until 2025.

In contrast, the Denny Way bus lane shows us how much that timeline can be compressed to prioritize transit riders sooner if the political support is there. Wilson and Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck even helped paint bus lane markings themselves in a press event in late August .

"This is an incredibly encouraging start. Route 8 carries more than 7,000 riders every day and connects Downtown, South Lake Union, Capitol Hill, the Central District, and Mount Baker," Wilson said. "These are not just numbers. Saving time on the bus means more predictable trips to work, school appointments, and of course, home to spend time with your family. That is what reliable transit should do: make it easier for people to get where they need to go."
In fact, some people have moved to Seattle in part because of the attraction of the city's fast-improving transit, as race participants told The Urbanist on Tuesday.
"I just moved here too, and I'm from the south, where they hate public transit," Melissa said. "And it's f*ing awesome. It's so cool to have it."
Melissa raced with Aubrey and her dog Lola. Aubrey moved to Seattle after living all over the country, most recently in Olympia.

"As soon as I moved here and started taking transit, I immediately noticed how quick [it is]," Aubrey said. "I just think the dedicated bus lanes are amazing in general, and I do take the 8, and it avoids this whole cluster right here, which is great on the bus-only lane."
Taylor, who lives in Belltown and participated in the race, said used to avoid the 8 because it was a miserable experience to ride it, but that's changed seemingly overnight.

"Well, I have Ubered instead of taking the 8 because it's the only bus ride that I would get sick on from all the traffic," Taylor said. "I get carsick easily, and the 8 is the only bus that I consistently get carsick. It's the stop and start that would make me really dizzy."
Now the only thing holding back Route 8 is its frequency.

Earlier this month, Metro was able to boost frequency on the route during the afternoons on weekdays, bumping headways from 15 minutes to 12 minutes. But buses are still very full on rush hour, likely leading many riders to envy the frequency on the popular RapidRide G Line along Madison Street.

The good news is that more Route 8 trips could be on the way next year, if Seattle voters sign onto Wilson's plan to phase in 100,000 more annual bus trips with a beefed-up Seattle Transit Measure in November.

With the impossible now achieved on Denny Way to the benefit of thousands of daily transit riders, City leaders will have to decide whether to roll with the momentum created here... or be left in the dust.

articles.author: <name>Meg van Huygen</name>
paras: We’re not going to say people don’t come to Seattle for the food, but they definitely come for the views. The Cascades to the east, the Olympics to the west, Mount Rainier to the south, and water everywhere you look. Thanks to exceptional restaurants that occupy some choice real estate, enjoying a multiple-course meal or award-winning fare while drinking in the sights is a piece of cake.
